parts.md: The biology lab at Kendriya Vidyalaya, Dehradun, had a dusty cupboard of preserved specimens with no labels. Ms Thapa gave Class 11 a challenge: 'Sort them using only the six questions.' Kabir picked up a dried sponge full of holes. 'No tissues, no symmetry, pores everywhere: Porifera.' A jar with a jellyfish-like blob and tentacles followed: 'Radial, two layers, stinging cells: Coelenterata.'

Next came three worms. Ananya flattened her palm beside the first: 'Flat, no body cavity, hooks on the head: a tapeworm, Platyhelminthes.' The second was round, smooth and long. 'Pseudocoelom, sexes separate: Ascaris.' The third had neat rings all along its body. 'Metameric segments, so Annelida. It's an earthworm.' The class applauded.

A crab, a cockroach and a scorpion were easy: jointed legs and a chitin shell, Arthropoda. A snail shell with a dried foot inside was Mollusca. A starfish brought the first argument. Rohan said it was radial, so it should be with the jellyfish. Ms Thapa smiled: 'Check the germ layers and the coelom. And look at its larva, which is bilateral.' They placed it in Echinodermata, with its water vascular system.

Finally the vertebrates: a shark embryo (cartilage, no operculum), a rohu (bony, air bladder), a frog (moist skin, three-chambered heart), a lizard (dry scales), a pigeon skeleton with hollow bones, and a bat with fur. 'Bat is a bird, it flies!' someone shouted. Ananya pointed to the hair and the mammary glands in the chart. 'Mammal.' The cupboard was finally sorted, and nobody had needed to memorise a million names.

workedExamples.q: Classify an animal that is bilateral, triploblastic, has a pseudocoelom, a complete gut and separate sexes.
steps: Triploblastic + bilateral rules out sponges, cnidarians, ctenophores.
Pseudocoelom is the key feature of Aschelminthes.
Complete gut and dioecious nature confirm it.

workedExamples.q: Identify the class: jawed, bony skeleton, operculum present, air bladder present, two-chambered heart.
steps: Jawed → Gnathostomata; fins and two-chambered heart → Pisces.
Bony skeleton and operculum → not Chondrichthyes.

workedExamples.q: Match the structure to its phylum: (a) comb plates (b) parapodia (c) radula (d) choanocytes (e) flame cells (f) Malpighian tubules.
steps: Flame cells → Platyhelminthes; Malpighian tubules → Arthropoda.
workedExamples.answer: (a) Ctenophora (b) Annelida (c) Mollusca (d) Porifera (e) Platyhelminthes (f) Arthropoda

summary: Basis of classification: organisation level, symmetry, germ layers, coelom, segmentation, notochord.
Cellular (sponges) → tissue (cnidarians) → organ (flatworms) → organ system (annelids onwards).
Diploblastic: cnidarians, ctenophores; triploblastic: flatworms to chordates.
Acoelomate: platyhelminthes; pseudocoelomate: aschelminthes; coelomate: annelids onward.
Porifera: canal system, ostia, osculum, choanocytes, spicules; hermaphrodite.
Coelenterata: cnidoblasts, polyp and medusa, metagenesis in Obelia; Ctenophora: eight comb plates, bioluminescence.
Platyhelminthes: flame cells, hooks/suckers; Aschelminthes: dioecious, complete gut; Annelida: metamerism, nephridia, closed circulation.
Arthropoda is the largest phylum: jointed legs, chitin, Malpighian tubules, open circulation.
Mollusca: shell, mantle, foot, radula; Echinodermata: water vascular system, radial adults; Hemichordata: proboscis, collar, trunk.
Chordates: notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal gill slits, post-anal tail.
All vertebrates are chordates but not all chordates are vertebrates.
Fishes have 2-chambered hearts, amphibians and most reptiles 3, crocodiles, birds and mammals 4.
Birds and mammals are homoiothermous; mammals have hair, pinnae and mammary glands.

glossary.d: Alternation between polyp (asexual) and medusa (sexual) forms in some cnidarians.
Animal whose body temperature changes with surroundings (cold-blooded).
Animal that keeps a constant body temperature (warm-blooded).
Common chamber into which gut, urinary and reproductive ducts open.
Hollow air-filled bones of birds.

rd-school-c11-biology-a.ch05-morphology-.title: Morphology of Flowering Plants
rd-school-c11-biology-a.ch05-morphology-.subtitle: Roots, stems, leaves, flowers, fruits and seeds — and how to describe a plant like a botanist
tags: Structural Organisation in Plants and Animals

sections.h: Reading a plant like a book
sections.md:
Pick up a mustard plant from a winter field in Haryana. A pale root holds it to the soil. A green stem rises, carrying leaves, then a cluster of yellow flowers, and lower down, slender pods full of seeds. Now pick up a wheat plant: a tuft of thin roots, a hollow stem, long narrow leaves with parallel veins, and an ear of grain. Both are angiosperms, yet almost every part looks different.

**Morphology** is the study of the external form and features of organisms. In plants, morphology gives us a precise vocabulary for describing those differences, and this vocabulary is the foundation of plant classification. When a botanist writes 'leaves alternate, simple, reticulate venation; flowers actinomorphic, pentamerous, hypogynous', a trained reader can picture the plant without seeing it.

The body of a typical flowering plant has two systems:

- the **root system**, mostly underground, and
- the **shoot system** — stem, branches, leaves, flowers and fruits — above the ground.

We will go part by part, in the order the plant itself builds them: root, stem, leaf, inflorescence, flower, fruit, seed. Then we will learn to write a **semi-technical description** and a **floral formula**, and apply them to three important families: **Fabaceae**, **Solanaceae** and **Liliaceae**.

Keep in mind one big idea through the whole chapter: **the same basic organ can be modified** for very different jobs — storage, support, climbing, protection, even catching insects. Recognising the organ behind the disguise is the real skill.

check.q: Morphology of plants is the study of:
check.why: Morphology deals with the external form; the internal structure is the subject of anatomy, covered in the next chapter.

sections.md:
In most dicots, the **radicle** (embryonic root) elongates directly to form the **primary root**, which grows into the soil. It bears lateral roots of several orders — secondary, tertiary and so on. The primary root and its branches form the **tap root system**, as in mustard. In monocots, the primary root is short-lived and replaced by a large number of roots originating from the base of the stem; these form the **fibrous root system**, as in wheat. In some plants like grass, *Monstera* and the banyan, roots arise from parts of the plant other than the radicle: these are **adventitious roots**.

The main functions of roots are absorbing water and minerals, anchoring the plant, storing reserve food and synthesising plant growth regulators.

**Regions of the root.** The tip is covered by a thimble-like **root cap** that protects the tender apex as it pushes through soil. A few millimetres above it lies the **region of meristematic activity** — small, thin-walled cells with dense protoplasm that divide repeatedly. Cells just behind this rapidly lengthen: the **region of elongation**, responsible for growth in length. These cells gradually differentiate and mature: the **region of maturation**, from which very fine, delicate thread-like **root hairs** arise. Root hairs absorb water and minerals from soil.

**Modifications.** Roots change shape to do other jobs.

- **Storage**: tap roots of **carrot** and **turnip**, and adventitious roots of **sweet potato**, swell with food.
- **Support**: **prop roots** of banyan hang down from branches and become pillars; **stilt roots** of **maize** and **sugarcane** arise from lower stem nodes.
- **Respiration**: in swampy areas, plants like *Rhizophora* (a mangrove) grow roots vertically upwards out of the mud — **pneumatophores** — to get oxygen.

sections.md:
The **stem** is the ascending part of the axis bearing branches, leaves, flowers and fruits. It develops from the **plumule** of the embryo. It bears **nodes** — regions where leaves are born — and **internodes**, the portions between two nodes. It carries buds, terminal or axillary. The stem is green when young and often becomes woody and dark brown later.

Its main job is to spread out branches bearing leaves, flowers and fruits, and to conduct water, minerals and food. Some stems also store food, support the plant, protect it, or help in vegetative propagation.

**Underground stems for storage** (they survive bad seasons and also propagate): **potato** (tuber — note the 'eyes' are buds at nodes), **ginger** and **turmeric** (rhizomes), *Colocasia* (arbi) and **onion** (bulb with fleshy leaf bases on a short disc-like stem). How do we know a potato is a stem and not a root? It has nodes with buds and scale leaves — roots never do.

**Tendrils** develop from axillary buds and are slender, spirally coiled, helping plants climb: gourds (cucumber, pumpkins, watermelon) and grapevines.

**Thorns** are axillary buds modified into woody, straight, pointed structures that protect plants from browsing animals: *Citrus*, *Bougainvillea*.

**Flattened green stems** in arid regions: *Opuntia* has a flattened stem (phylloclade) that photosynthesises; *Euphorbia* has a fleshy cylindrical one. Both reduce water loss since true leaves are reduced to spines.

**Sub-aerial stems for spreading**: in grass and strawberry, lateral branches arise from the base of the main axis, grow horizontally above the ground, then turn down to root (**runners**). In *Pistia* (water lettuce) and *Eichhornia* (water hyacinth), a lateral branch with short internodes ends in a rosette of leaves and a tuft of roots (**offset**). In banana, pineapple and *Chrysanthemum*, lateral branches originate from the basal and underground portion of the main stem, grow obliquely upward and give rise to leafy shoots (**suckers**).
keyTerms: Node / internode — leaf-bearing point / space between two nodes
Rhizome — horizontal underground stem (ginger)
Phylloclade — flattened green stem (Opuntia)
Sucker — underground lateral branch rising as a new shoot (banana)

sections.h: The leaf: venation, types and phyllotaxy
sections.md:
The **leaf** is a lateral, generally flattened structure borne on the stem. It develops at the node and bears a bud in its axil; the axillary bud later develops into a branch. Leaves originate from **shoot apical meristems** and are arranged in an **acropetal** order (younger ones near the apex). They are the most important vegetative organs for photosynthesis.

A typical leaf has three main parts:

1. **Leaf base** — attaches the leaf to the stem; may bear two small lateral leaf-like **stipules**. In monocots the leaf base expands into a **sheath** covering the stem partly or wholly. In some legumes the leaf base becomes swollen — the **pulvinus**.
2. **Petiole** — holds the blade to light; long thin flexible petioles let blades flutter in wind, cooling the leaf and bringing fresh air to the surface.
3. **Lamina** (leaf blade) — the green expanded part with **veins** and **veinlets**. A prominent vein, the **midrib**, runs in the middle. Veins provide rigidity and act as channels of transport.

**Venation.** The arrangement of veins and veinlets in the lamina. When veinlets form a network, it is **reticulate venation** (most dicots). When veins run parallel within a lamina, it is **parallel venation** (most monocots).

**Types of leaves.** A leaf is **simple** when its lamina is entire or, when incised, the incisions do not touch the midrib. When incisions reach up to the midrib, breaking the lamina into a number of **leaflets**, the leaf is **compound**. A bud is present in the axil of the petiole in both simple and compound leaves, but **not in the axil of leaflets**. In a **pinnately compound** leaf, a number of leaflets are present on a common axis, the **rachis**, which represents the midrib — as in neem. In **palmately compound** leaves, leaflets are attached at a common point, the tip of the petiole — as in silk cotton.

**Phyllotaxy** is the pattern of arrangement of leaves on the stem or branch: **alternate** (a single leaf at each node in alternate manner — china rose, mustard, sunflower), **opposite** (a pair of leaves at each node opposite each other — *Calotropis*, guava), **whorled** (more than two leaves at a node forming a whorl — *Alstonia*).

**Modifications.** Leaves become **tendrils** for climbing (peas), **spines** for defence (cacti), fleshy storage leaves (onion, garlic), and in some plants like Australian *Acacia*, leaves are small and short-lived while **petioles expand, become green** and photosynthesise. In insectivorous plants such as the **pitcher plant** and **Venus flytrap**, leaves are modified to trap insects.

check.q: How can you tell a compound leaf from a branch bearing simple leaves?
options: The compound leaf has a bud only in the axil of its petiole, not of its leaflets
check.why: A bud sits in the axil of the whole leaf's petiole, but never in the axil of individual leaflets, whereas each simple leaf on a branch has its own axillary bud.

sections.md:
A **flower** is a modified shoot in which the shoot apical meristem changes to floral meristem; internodes do not elongate, and the axis gets condensed. The apex produces different kinds of floral appendages laterally at successive nodes instead of leaves. The arrangement of flowers on the floral axis is the **inflorescence**. In **racemose** inflorescences the main axis continues to grow, and flowers are borne laterally in **acropetal succession** (older below, younger above). In **cymose** inflorescences the main axis terminates in a flower and so is limited in growth; flowers are borne in **basipetal** order.

The flower is the reproductive unit of angiosperms. It typically has four whorls on a swollen end of the stalk (pedicel), the **thalamus** or receptacle: **calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium**. Calyx and corolla are accessory organs; androecium and gynoecium are reproductive. In some flowers like lily, calyx and corolla are not distinct and are called **perianth**. A flower with both androecium and gynoecium is **bisexual**; one with only stamens or only carpels is **unisexual**.

**Symmetry.** A flower is **actinomorphic** (radially symmetrical) when it can be divided into two equal radial halves in any radial plane through the centre — mustard, datura, chilli. It is **zygomorphic** (bilaterally symmetrical) when it can be divided into two similar halves only in one particular vertical plane — pea, gulmohur, bean, *Cassia*. An **asymmetric** flower cannot be divided into two similar halves by any vertical plane — canna.

Flowers may be **trimerous, tetramerous or pentamerous** when floral appendages are in multiples of 3, 4 or 5. Flowers with **bracts** (reduced leaves at the base of the pedicel) are bracteate; those without, ebracteate.

**Position of floral parts on the thalamus.**

- **Hypogynous** — gynoecium at the highest position; other parts below it. Ovary is **superior** (mustard, china rose, brinjal).
- **Perigynous** — gynoecium in the centre and other parts on the rim of the thalamus at almost the same level. Ovary is **half-inferior** (plum, rose, peach).
- **Epigynous** — the margin of the thalamus grows upward, enclosing the ovary completely and fusing with it; other parts arise above the ovary. Ovary is **inferior** (guava, cucumber, ray florets of sunflower).

check.why: Guava flowers are epigynous: the thalamus encloses and fuses with the ovary, so the ovary lies below the other parts.

sections.h: Parts of a flower in detail
sections.md:
**Calyx** — the outermost whorl; its members are **sepals**, generally green and leaf-like, protecting the flower in bud. It may be **gamosepalous** (sepals united) or **polysepalous** (free).

**Corolla** — made of **petals**, usually brightly coloured to attract insects for pollination. Gamopetalous or polypetalous. Shape varies: tubular, bell-shaped, funnel-shaped or wheel-shaped.

**Aestivation** — the mode of arrangement of sepals or petals in the floral bud with respect to other members of the same whorl:

- **Valvate** — sepals or petals just touch one another at the margin without overlapping (*Calotropis*).
- **Twisted** — one margin of each appendage overlaps that of the next one, and so on (china rose, lady's finger, cotton).
- **Imbricate** — margins overlap but not in any particular direction (*Cassia*, gulmohur).
- **Vexillary (papilionaceous)** — in pea and bean, five petals: the largest (**standard**) overlaps the two lateral petals (**wings**), which in turn overlap the two smallest anterior petals (**keel**).

**Androecium** — composed of **stamens**, the male reproductive organ. Each stamen has a stalk or **filament** and an **anther**. Each anther is usually bilobed and each lobe has two chambers, the **pollen sacs**, where pollen grains form. A sterile stamen is a **staminode**. When stamens are attached to petals they are **epipetalous** (brinjal); attached to perianth, **epiphyllous** (lily). Stamens may be free (**polyandrous**) or united in varying degrees: into one bunch (**monoadelphous**, china rose), two bundles (**diadelphous**, pea), or more than two (**polyadelphous**, citrus). Filament length may vary within a flower (*Salvia*, mustard).

**Gynoecium** — the female reproductive part, made of one or more **carpels**. A carpel has three parts: **stigma** (receptive surface for pollen), **style** (elongated tube) and **ovary** (enlarged basal part bearing ovules on a flattened cushion, the **placenta**). When more than one carpel is present, they may be free (**apocarpous**, lotus and rose) or fused (**syncarpous**, mustard and tomato). After fertilisation, ovules develop into seeds and the ovary matures into a fruit.

**Placentation** — the arrangement of ovules within the ovary:

- **Marginal** — placenta forms a ridge along the ventral suture of the ovary; ovules in two rows (pea).
- **Axile** — placenta is axial and ovules attached to it in a multilocular ovary (china rose, tomato, lemon).
- **Parietal** — ovules develop on the inner wall of the ovary or peripheral part; ovary one-chambered but becomes two-chambered by a false septum (mustard, *Argemone*).
- **Free central** — ovules borne on a central axis and septa absent (*Dianthus*, *Primrose*).
- **Basal** — placenta develops at the base of the ovary and a single ovule is attached (sunflower, marigold).

sections.md:
The **fruit** is a characteristic feature of flowering plants: a mature or ripened ovary, developed after fertilisation. If a fruit forms without fertilisation of the ovary, it is a **parthenocarpic** fruit (like seedless banana varieties). A fruit consists of a wall or **pericarp** and seeds. The pericarp may be dry or fleshy. When thick and fleshy, it is differentiated into the outer **epicarp**, the middle **mesocarp** and the inner **endocarp**.

In **mango** and **coconut** the fruit is a **drupe**: developing from a monocarpellary superior ovary, one-seeded. In mango the pericarp is well differentiated into a thin epicarp, fleshy edible mesocarp and a stony hard endocarp. In coconut, the mesocarp is **fibrous** (coir).

**The seed.** Ovules after fertilisation develop into seeds. A seed is made of a **seed coat** and an **embryo**. The embryo has a radicle, an embryonal axis and one (wheat, maize) or two (gram, pea) cotyledons.

**Dicot seed (e.g. gram, bean).** The outermost covering is the seed coat, with two layers: outer **testa** and inner **tegmen**. The **hilum** is a scar where the developing seed was attached to the fruit. Above the hilum is a small pore, the **micropyle**. Within the seed coat is the embryo: an embryonal axis and two fleshy cotyledons, which store food. At the two ends of the axis are the **radicle** and **plumule**. In some seeds like castor, the **endosperm** formed by double fertilisation is a food-storing tissue (endospermic seeds). In bean, gram and pea, the endosperm is absent in mature seeds (non-endospermous).

**Monocot seed (e.g. maize).** Generally **endospermic**, though some (orchids) are non-endospermic. In cereals like maize, the seed coat is membranous and generally fused with the fruit wall. The endosperm is bulky and stores food. Its outer covering is a proteinous layer, the **aleurone layer**. The embryo is small and situated in a groove at one end of the endosperm. It has one large, shield-shaped cotyledon, the **scutellum**, and a short axis with plumule and radicle. The plumule and radicle are enclosed in sheaths called **coleoptile** and **coleorhiza** respectively.

**Did you know?** The single coconut 'seed' with its watery endosperm (coconut water) is one of the largest seeds that floats — coconuts can drift across oceans and still germinate on a new beach.

check.q: In a maize grain, the plumule is enclosed in a sheath called:
check.why: The coleoptile sheathes the plumule; the coleorhiza covers the radicle, and the scutellum is the single cotyledon.

sections.h: Describing a plant: floral formula and three families
sections.md:
A flowering plant is described in a sequence: habit, vegetative characters (roots, stem, leaves), then floral characters (inflorescence and flower parts). The flower is summarised by a **floral diagram** and a **floral formula**, using symbols:

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Br | bracteate |
| K | calyx |
| C | corolla |
| P | perianth |
| A | androecium |
| G | gynoecium |
| G with a line above the number | inferior ovary |
| G with a line below the number | superior ovary |
| ⚥ | bisexual; ♂ male, ♀ female |
| ⊕ | actinomorphic; % zygomorphic |
| (number) in brackets | fused (e.g. K(5) = 5 united sepals) |

Fusion between whorls is shown by an arc linking the symbols, e.g. epipetalous stamens.

**Fabaceae** (earlier a sub-family Papilionoideae of Leguminosae). Trees, shrubs, herbs; roots with **root nodules**. Leaves alternate, pinnately compound or simple; leaf base pulvinate, stipulate. Inflorescence racemose. Flowers bisexual, **zygomorphic**. Calyx: five sepals, gamosepalous, imbricate. Corolla: five petals, polypetalous, papilionaceous (standard, two wings, two keels). Androecium: ten, **diadelphous** (9 + 1), anther dithecous. Gynoecium: ovary superior, **monocarpellary**, unilocular with many ovules, style single. Fruit: **legume**; seed one to many, non-endospermic. Floral formula: % ⚥ K(5) C1+2+(2) A(9)+1 G1 (superior). Economic importance: pulses (gram, arhar, moong, soybean), edible oil (soybean, groundnut), dyes (indigofera), fibres (sunhemp), fodder (*Sesbania*, *Trifolium*), ornamentals (lupin, sweet pea), medicine (muliathi).

**Solanaceae** — the 'potato family'. Mostly herbs, shrubs, small trees. Stem herbaceous, rarely woody, aerial, erect, cylindrical, branched, solid or hollow, hairy or glabrous; underground stem in potato. Leaves alternate, simple, rarely pinnately compound, exstipulate, reticulate venation. Inflorescence solitary, axillary or cymose as in *Solanum*. Flowers bisexual, **actinomorphic**. Calyx: five sepals, united, persistent, valvate. Corolla: five petals, united, valvate. Androecium: five stamens, **epipetalous**. Gynoecium: **bicarpellary**, obliquely placed, syncarpous; ovary superior, bilocular, placenta swollen with many ovules, **axile**. Fruit: berry or capsule; seeds many, endospermous. Floral formula: ⊕ ⚥ K(5) C(5) A5 (epipetalous) G(2) superior. Economic importance: food (tomato, brinjal, potato), spice (chilli), medicine (belladonna, *Ashwagandha*), fumigatory (tobacco), ornamentals (petunia).

**Liliaceae** — the 'lily family', a characteristic monocot family. Mostly perennial herbs with underground bulbs, corms or rhizomes. Leaves mostly basal, alternate, linear, exstipulate, parallel venation. Inflorescence solitary or cymose; often umbellate clusters. Flowers bisexual, actinomorphic. Perianth: six tepals (3 + 3), often united into a tube; valvate aestivation. Androecium: six stamens, 3 + 3, **epitepalous**. Gynoecium: **tricarpellary**, syncarpous, ovary superior, trilocular with many ovules, axile placentation. Fruit: capsule, rarely berry; seed endospermous. Floral formula: ⊕ ⚥ P(3+3) A3+3 G(3) superior. Economic importance: ornamentals (tulip, *Gloriosa*), medicine (*Aloe*), vegetables (*Asparagus*), and colchicine (from *Colchicum autumnale*).

check.q: The floral formula ⊕ ⚥ K(5) C(5) A5 G(2) with a superior ovary and epipetalous stamens belongs to:
check.why: Solanaceae flowers are actinomorphic and pentamerous with fused sepals and petals, five epipetalous stamens and a bicarpellary superior ovary.

workedExamples.q: A plant has fleshy underground parts with nodes, buds ('eyes') and scale leaves. Is it a root or a stem? Name an example.
steps: Roots never bear nodes or buds.
Nodes, buds and scale leaves are diagnostic of stems.
So the swollen part is an underground stem tuber.

workedExamples.q: Write the floral formula of a flower that is zygomorphic, bisexual, with 5 fused sepals, 1 standard + 2 wings + 2 fused keel petals, 9+1 stamens and one superior carpel.
steps: Androecium A(9)+1 diadelphous; gynoecium G1, superior.

summary: Tap roots (dicots) come from the radicle; fibrous roots (monocots) from the stem base; adventitious roots from other parts.
Root regions: root cap, meristematic zone, elongation, maturation (root hairs).
Root modifications: storage (carrot, sweet potato), prop (banyan), stilt (maize), pneumatophores (Rhizophora).
Stems bear nodes and internodes; modified into tubers, rhizomes, bulbs, tendrils, thorns, phylloclades, runners, offsets, suckers.
Leaf: base, petiole, lamina; reticulate vs parallel venation; simple vs pinnately/palmately compound.
Phyllotaxy: alternate, opposite, whorled.
Racemose inflorescences grow on with acropetal flowers; cymose ones end in a flower (basipetal).
Flower whorls: calyx, corolla, androecium, gynoecium on the thalamus; actinomorphic, zygomorphic or asymmetric.
Hypogynous (superior ovary), perigynous (half-inferior), epigynous (inferior).
Aestivation: valvate, twisted, imbricate, vexillary; placentation: marginal, axile, parietal, free central, basal.
Fruit = ripened ovary; pericarp: epicarp, mesocarp, endocarp; mango and coconut are drupes.
Dicot seed: testa, tegmen, hilum, micropyle, two cotyledons; maize: aleurone layer, scutellum, coleoptile, coleorhiza.
Fabaceae, Solanaceae and Liliaceae can be recognised from their floral formulae.

rd-school-c11-biology-a.ch06-anatomy-flo.title: Anatomy of Flowering Plants
rd-school-c11-biology-a.ch06-anatomy-flo.subtitle: Slice a stem, look through a microscope, and find the hidden plumbing, armour and growth rings of plants
tags: Structural Organisation in Plants and Animals

sections.md:
In a school lab in Bhopal, a student takes a fresh sunflower stem and slices it thinner than a hair with a razor blade. She stains it pink with safranin and puts it under the microscope. The plain green stem turns into a tiny city: a neat ring of bundles, thick-walled support cells, a soft central pith and a waxy outer wall. She repeats the experiment with a maize stem, and this time the bundles are scattered all over, like stars in the night sky.

This is **plant anatomy**, the study of a plant's internal structure. The previous chapter looked at plants from the outside; now we look inside. Anatomy shows how each structure suits its job, and it also helps us classify plants, because monocots and dicots are as different inside as they are outside.

The chapter works from small to large:

1. **Tissues:** meristematic and permanent (simple and complex).
2. **Tissue systems:** epidermal, ground and vascular.
3. **Anatomy of organs:** roots, stems and leaves of dicots and monocots.
4. **Secondary growth:** how trees thicken and form wood, annual rings and bark.

A **tissue** is a group of cells that share an origin and usually do the same job. Plant tissues are sorted first by one question: can the cells still divide?

check.q: A tissue is best defined as a group of cells that:
options: Have a common origin and usually a common function
check.why: Cells of a tissue share their origin and generally work together on a common function.

sections.md:
Unlike animals, plants grow only in particular zones of active cell division called **meristems** (Greek *meristos*, divided).

- **Apical meristems** sit at the tips of roots and shoots and build the **primary tissues** that lengthen the plant. As the shoot tip grows and forms leaves, a few meristem cells are left behind in the angle (axil) of each leaf. These become **axillary buds**, which can later grow into a branch or a flower.
- **Intercalary meristems** lie between mature tissues, typically at the base of internodes and leaves in grasses. They regrow the parts eaten by grazing animals, which is why a lawn springs back after mowing.
- **Lateral meristems** run along the sides of mature roots and shoots, especially in woody plants. They produce **secondary tissues** that increase thickness (girth). Examples are the **fascicular vascular cambium**, the **interfascicular cambium** and the **cork cambium**.

Apical and intercalary meristems appear early in the plant's life and build the primary body, so they are called **primary meristems**. Lateral meristems appear later and are **secondary meristems**.

Once new cells stop dividing and become specialised for a job, they form **permanent** (mature) **tissues**.

check.q: Which meristem helps grass regrow after grazing?
check.why: The intercalary meristem at the base of grass internodes and leaves restores the parts eaten or cut.

sections.md:
**Simple tissues** contain only one kind of cell.

- **Parenchyma** is the 'general-purpose' tissue and makes up most of the inside of organs. Its cells are roughly equal in all directions (round, oval or many-sided, sometimes elongated), with thin cellulose walls. They may be packed tightly or have small air spaces between them. Parenchyma photosynthesises, stores food and secretes substances.
- **Collenchyma** forms layers or patches just under the epidermis in **dicots**. Its living cells have walls **thickened at the corners** with cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin, and often contain chloroplasts. There are no air spaces between cells. It gives flexible **support** to growing parts such as young stems and leaf stalks (petioles).
- **Sclerenchyma** has cells with **thick walls hardened by lignin**, crossed by pits. The cells are usually **dead** when mature. There are two types. **Fibres** are long, narrow and pointed, and usually occur in bundles. **Sclereids** are short, round or oval, so heavily thickened that the cell cavity (lumen) is almost gone. Sclereids make nut shells hard, the pulp of guava and pear gritty, and also occur in legume seed coats and tea leaves. Sclerenchyma gives **rigid mechanical support**.

> Did you know? The 'sand' you feel when you bite a guava is a crowd of sclereids, so you are chewing a plant's armour.

check.q: Which simple tissue has living cells with walls thickened mainly at the corners?
check.why: Collenchyma cells are alive and have cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin deposited at their corners, giving flexible support.

sections.md:
**Complex tissues** contain several kinds of cells working as a team. The two complex tissues are **xylem** and **phloem**.

**Xylem** carries water and minerals up from the roots to the stem and leaves, and also strengthens the plant. It has four kinds of cells:

- **Tracheids:** long, dead cells with thick lignified walls and tapering ends. Their inner walls carry thickenings in various patterns.
- **Vessels:** long tubes made of many dead cells (**vessel members**) joined end to end. The end walls are perforated, leaving a wide open channel. **Vessels are a hallmark of angiosperms**; gymnosperms generally lack them. In flowering plants, tracheids and vessels together are the main water pipes.
- **Xylem fibres:** very thick walls with an almost closed lumen. They may be divided by cross-walls (septate) or not (aseptate).
- **Xylem parenchyma:** the only living cells in xylem. They store starch, fat and tannins, and **ray parenchyma** moves water sideways (radially).

The xylem that forms first is **protoxylem**, and the later xylem is **metaxylem**. In stems, protoxylem lies towards the centre (pith): this is **endarch**. In roots, protoxylem lies towards the outside: this is **exarch**.

**Phloem** carries food, usually from the leaves to the rest of the plant. In angiosperms it has **sieve tube elements, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and phloem fibres**. Gymnosperms have **sieve cells and albuminous cells** instead of sieve tubes and companion cells.

- **Sieve tube elements** are long cells joined end to end. Their end walls are perforated like a sieve, forming **sieve plates**. A mature sieve element is alive, with cytoplasm and a large vacuole, but it has **no nucleus**. The nucleus of the neighbouring companion cell controls it.
- **Companion cells** are specialised parenchyma cells joined to sieve elements by pit fields. They help maintain the pressure that drives food through the sieve tubes.
- **Phloem parenchyma** stores food, resins, latex and mucilage. It is missing in most monocots.
- **Phloem (bast) fibres** are sclerenchyma cells. They are usually absent in primary phloem but common in secondary phloem. Jute, flax and hemp fibres are bast fibres, which is why West Bengal's jute mills depend on phloem.

keyTerms: Endarch — protoxylem towards the centre (stems)
Exarch — protoxylem towards the periphery (roots)
Sieve plate — perforated end wall of a sieve tube
Sclereid — short, very thick-walled dead cell (grit in guava)

check.q: Which of these lacks a nucleus when mature but is still living?
check.why: Mature sieve tube elements have cytoplasm but no nucleus; their activities are regulated by the companion cell's nucleus. Tracheids and vessels are dead.

sections.md:
Tissues can also be grouped by where they lie in the plant, giving three **tissue systems**.

**1. Epidermal tissue system:** the plant's skin. It includes epidermal cells, stomata and outgrowths such as hairs. The **epidermis** is usually a single layer of tightly packed, elongated parenchyma cells, each with a large vacuole. On aerial parts it is often coated with a waxy **cuticle** that cuts down water loss. Roots have no cuticle.

**Stomata** are pores that control water loss (transpiration) and gas exchange. Each pore is surrounded by two **guard cells**. In most plants these are bean-shaped, but in grasses they are **dumb-bell-shaped**. The inner wall of each guard cell, facing the pore, is thick, while the outer wall is thin. This difference makes the pore open when the guard cells swell. Guard cells have chloroplasts. The neighbouring epidermal cells are sometimes specialised as **subsidiary cells**. The pore, guard cells and subsidiary cells together form the **stomatal apparatus**.

**Root hairs** are single-celled extensions of root epidermal cells that absorb water and minerals. Hairs on the stem, called **trichomes**, are usually many-celled and may be branched, soft, stiff or even glandular. They help reduce water loss.

**2. Ground tissue system:** everything except the epidermis and the vascular bundles. It is made of the simple tissues parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma. In young stems and roots it forms the cortex, pericycle, pith and medullary rays. In leaves it is the chloroplast-rich **mesophyll**.

**3. Vascular tissue system:** xylem and phloem grouped into **vascular bundles**.

- **Open** bundles have a strip of cambium between xylem and phloem, so they can make secondary tissues (dicot stems). **Closed** bundles have no cambium (monocots).
- **Radial** bundles have xylem and phloem on alternate radii (roots). **Conjoint** bundles have xylem and phloem on the same radius, usually with phloem outside (stems, leaves).

check.q: Vascular bundles of monocot stems are called 'closed' because:
check.why: With no cambium between xylem and phloem, monocot bundles cannot add secondary tissues, so they are closed.

sections.md:
**Dicot root (sunflower, bean).** From the outside inward:

- **Epiblema:** the outer layer, carrying single-celled root hairs.
- **Cortex:** many layers of thin-walled parenchyma with air spaces.
- **Endodermis:** the innermost layer of the cortex. Its barrel-shaped cells fit tightly together, and their radial and tangential walls carry bands of waterproof **suberin** called **Casparian strips**. These force water to pass through the living cells, so the root can control what enters.
- **Pericycle:** a few layers of thick-walled parenchyma. Lateral roots and, later, part of the vascular cambium start here.
- **Vascular bundles:** radial, usually **two to four** patches of xylem and phloem (diarch to tetrarch), with exarch xylem. Parenchyma between xylem and phloem is **conjunctive tissue**.
- **Pith:** small or absent.

Everything inside the endodermis (pericycle, vascular bundles and pith) makes up the **stele**. A cambium ring later forms between xylem and phloem.

**Monocot root (maize).** It has the same set of layers, but with **more than six xylem patches (polyarch)**, a **large pith** and **no secondary growth**.

check.q: Casparian strips are found in the:
check.why: Endodermal cells of roots have suberin bands on their radial and tangential walls, called Casparian strips.

sections.h: Stems and leaves: dicot and monocot
sections.md:
**Dicot stem (sunflower).**

- **Epidermis** with a thin cuticle, a few stomata and trichomes.
- **Cortex** in three zones: the **hypodermis** of collenchyma just under the epidermis, which gives young stems strength; general **cortical parenchyma**; and the innermost **endodermis**, full of starch grains and therefore called the **starch sheath**.
- **Pericycle** as half-moon (semi-lunar) caps of sclerenchyma above each phloem patch.
- **Medullary rays** of parenchyma between bundles.
- **Vascular bundles arranged in a ring.** Each is **conjoint, open, with endarch protoxylem**. The ring arrangement is the dicot signature.
- A large **pith** of round parenchyma cells with air spaces.

**Monocot stem (maize).** A **sclerenchymatous hypodermis**, many **scattered** vascular bundles each wrapped in a **sclerenchyma bundle sheath**, and plenty of ground parenchyma. The bundles are **conjoint and closed**; those near the edge are smaller than those in the centre. There is no phloem parenchyma, and each bundle has a **water-containing cavity**.

**Dorsiventral (dicot) leaf.** A vertical section shows epidermis, mesophyll and veins. The upper (**adaxial**) and lower (**abaxial**) epidermis both carry a cuticle, but the lower one has **more stomata**, and the upper may have none. The mesophyll has two types:

- **palisade parenchyma**, tall cells standing side by side under the upper surface, packed with chloroplasts;
- **spongy parenchyma**, loose, rounded cells with large air spaces, reaching down to the lower epidermis.

Veins contain vascular bundles wrapped in thick-walled **bundle sheath** cells. Bundle size depends on the vein, because reticulate venation has veins of many sizes.

**Isobilateral (monocot) leaf.** Stomata are on **both surfaces**, and the mesophyll is **not divided** into palisade and spongy layers. In grasses, some upper epidermal cells along the veins are large, empty and colourless. These are **bulliform cells**. When they are full of water the leaf lies flat; when water is short they go limp and the leaf **rolls inward**, reducing water loss. Parallel venation shows up as bundles of nearly equal size.

check.why: When bulliform cells lose water they become flaccid and the leaf rolls up, reducing the area exposed to drying air.

sections.h: Dicot vs monocot: the identification table
sections.md:
Practical exams often hand you an unlabelled slide. Work through this table feature by feature, and you can name almost any primary root, stem or leaf section.

| Organ | Feature | Dicot | Monocot |
|---|---|---|---|
| Root | Xylem patches | 2–4 (diarch–tetrarch) | more than 6 (polyarch) |
| Root | Pith | small or absent | large, well developed |
| Root | Secondary growth | present | absent |
| Stem | Bundle arrangement | ring | scattered |
| Stem | Bundle type | conjoint, open | conjoint, closed, with sheath |
| Stem | Hypodermis | collenchyma | sclerenchyma |
| Stem | Ground tissue | cortex, endodermis, pericycle, pith distinct | undifferentiated ground tissue |
| Leaf | Type | dorsiventral | isobilateral |
| Leaf | Mesophyll | palisade + spongy | undifferentiated |
| Leaf | Stomata | mostly lower surface | both surfaces |
| Leaf | Bulliform cells | absent | present (grasses) |

A quick rule for stems: *ring and open → dicot; scattered, sheathed and closed → monocot*. For roots, count the xylem arms.

left.title: Dicot (sunflower, bean)
points: Stem bundles in a ring, open

check.q: A root section shows 12 xylem patches and a large pith. It is a:
check.why: Polyarch xylem (more than six patches) with a large pith is typical of monocot roots such as maize.

sections.h: Secondary growth: vascular cambium and wood
sections.md:
Growth in length from apical meristems is **primary growth**. Dicots and gymnosperms also grow thicker, which is **secondary growth**. It depends on two lateral meristems: the **vascular cambium** and the **cork cambium**.

**Forming the cambium ring.** In a young dicot stem, a strip of cambium already lies inside each bundle between xylem and phloem. This is the **intrafascicular cambium**. The medullary-ray cells next to it start dividing and become the **interfascicular cambium**. The two join to make a **complete ring**.

**What the ring makes.** The ring divides in both directions. Cells cut off on the inside become **secondary xylem**, and cells cut off on the outside become **secondary phloem**. The cambium works harder on the inner side, so far more xylem builds up than phloem. As the xylem piles up, the older primary and secondary phloem gets crushed. The primary xylem stays more or less intact near the centre. Here and there, the cambium also makes narrow radial bands of parenchyma, the **secondary medullary rays**, which carry materials sideways.

**Spring wood and autumn wood.** Cambial activity follows the seasons. In spring, when water and warmth are plentiful, the cambium makes many xylem cells with wide cavities. This **spring (early) wood** is light in colour and less dense. In winter it slows down and makes fewer cells with narrow vessels. This **autumn (late) wood** is darker and denser. One band of each makes an **annual ring**, and counting the rings estimates a tree's age. This method is **dendrochronology**. Ring width also records past rainfall and climate.

**Heartwood and sapwood.** In old trees, the central wood darkens as tannins, resins, oils, gums and aromatic substances fill it. This **heartwood** is made of dead, heavily lignified cells. It no longer carries water, but it is hard, long-lasting, resists insects and microbes, and holds the tree up. Good teak and sheesham furniture is made from heartwood. The lighter outer wood, **sapwood**, still carries water and minerals from root to leaf.

check.q: Why do annual rings form in temperate trees?
options: Cambium is equally active all year
Cambium makes wide-vessel spring wood and narrow-vessel autumn wood alternately

sections.h: Cork cambium, bark and secondary growth in roots
sections.md:
**Cork cambium.** As the stem widens, the old epidermis and outer cortex stretch, crack and must be replaced. A new meristem, the **cork cambium (phellogen)**, arises, usually in the cortex. It is a thin layer, a couple of cells thick, of narrow, roughly rectangular, thin-walled cells, and it divides in both directions:

- cells formed on the outside become **cork (phellem)**. Their walls are soaked with **suberin**, so cork is waterproof and protects the stem;
- cells formed on the inside become **secondary cortex (phelloderm)**.

Phellogen, phellem and phelloderm together form the **periderm**. In some places the phellogen makes loosely packed parenchyma instead of cork. These cells push out and burst the epidermis, forming lens-shaped pores called **lenticels**. Lenticels let gases pass between the air and the living tissues inside, and most woody trees have them.

**Bark** is an everyday word, not a technical term. It means everything outside the vascular cambium, including secondary phloem and periderm. Bark formed early in the season is **soft (early) bark**, and bark formed late is **hard (late) bark**. Cinnamon is a dried bark, and the cork of bottle stoppers comes from the cork oak.

**Secondary growth in dicot roots.** Here the vascular cambium is **entirely secondary**. It forms from strips of tissue just below each phloem bundle, joined by parts of the pericycle opposite the protoxylem. The resulting ring is first **wavy** and later becomes round. After that, the process is the same as in the stem.

Secondary growth also happens in the stems and roots of gymnosperms, but **usually not in monocots**. Palms and bamboos grow tall without true wood rings.
keyTerms: Periderm — phellem + phellogen + phelloderm
Lenticel — lens-shaped pore in bark for gas exchange
Dendrochronology — dating by counting annual rings
Heartwood — dark, non-conducting central wood

check.q: The periderm consists of:
check.why: Cork cambium (phellogen) produces cork (phellem) outside and secondary cortex (phelloderm) inside; together they form the periderm.

parts.md: Outside a village school near Vadodara stood a banyan said to be two hundred years old. When a storm brought down one branch, the science teacher, Mr Desai, brought a smooth cut slice to class. 'This is the tree's diary,' he said. 'Every ring is one year it has written down.' The students began counting from the dark centre outwards.

Some rings were wide and pale, others thin and dark. 'Wide pale bands are spring wood, made when the cambium had plenty of water,' Mr Desai explained. 'In the thin years, perhaps the monsoon failed.' Priya noticed three thin rings close together and checked the village records. There had been a long drought around that time. The tree had recorded it.

Under the microscope, a thin slice of a young twig from the same tree showed a ring of open bundles, a starch sheath and a pith, the signs of a dicot. On the bark, small raised dots were lenticels, where the tree breathes through its cork. 'And the hard dark centre that termites can't eat?' asked Arjun. 'Heartwood: dead cells full of resins and tannins. It no longer carries water, but it holds the whole tree up.'

By the end of the lesson, the class had read the banyan's life from the inside: meristems at its tips that made it taller, cambium that made it wider, xylem and phloem moving water and food, and cork protecting it from the outside. Priya wrote in her notebook: 'Every slice of a plant shows how it has lived.'

workedExamples.q: A section shows: conjoint, scattered bundles each with a sclerenchymatous sheath, no phloem parenchyma, water cavities in bundles. Identify it.
steps: Scattered bundles → not a dicot stem.
Conjoint bundles → stem, not root (roots have radial bundles).
Sheaths, no phloem parenchyma, water cavities → classic monocot features.

workedExamples.q: A tree trunk shows 28 annual rings and the cambium is still active. Estimate its age, and say which part conducts water.
steps: Each annual ring = one spring wood + one autumn wood band = 1 year.
The outer, lighter secondary xylem (sapwood) conducts water.

workedExamples.q: Arrange from outside to inside in an old dicot stem: secondary xylem, phellem, vascular cambium, phelloderm, secondary phloem, phellogen, primary xylem, pith.
steps: Periderm is outermost: phellem → phellogen → phelloderm.
Then secondary phloem → vascular cambium → secondary xylem.
Primary xylem near the centre, pith innermost.
workedExamples.answer: Phellem → phellogen → phelloderm → secondary phloem → vascular cambium → secondary xylem → primary xylem → pith

summary: Meristems: apical (length), intercalary (grasses), lateral (girth: vascular and cork cambium).
Simple permanent tissues: parenchyma, collenchyma (corner thickening, dicots), sclerenchyma (fibres, sclereids, dead).
Xylem: tracheids, vessels, xylem fibres, xylem parenchyma; vessels are characteristic of angiosperms.
Endarch protoxylem in stems, exarch in roots.
Phloem: sieve tubes (no nucleus), companion cells, phloem parenchyma, bast fibres; gymnosperms have sieve cells and albuminous cells.
Tissue systems: epidermal (cuticle, stomata, hairs), ground, vascular.
Dumb-bell guard cells in grasses; bean-shaped in dicots; subsidiary cells form the stomatal apparatus.
Radial bundles in roots; conjoint bundles in stems and leaves; open (with cambium) in dicots, closed in monocots.
Dicot root: 2–4 xylem patches, Casparian strips, small pith; monocot root: polyarch, large pith.
Dicot stem: ring of open bundles, starch sheath; monocot stem: scattered closed bundles with bundle sheaths.
Dorsiventral leaf has palisade and spongy mesophyll; isobilateral leaf has stomata on both sides and bulliform cells.
Vascular cambium produces more secondary xylem; annual rings of spring and autumn wood give tree age.
Heartwood is dark and non-conducting; sapwood conducts.
Cork cambium forms periderm (phellem, phellogen, phelloderm) and lenticels; bark is everything outside the vascular cambium.

glossary.d: All tissues inside the endodermis: pericycle, vascular bundles and pith.
Parenchyma lying between xylem and phloem in roots.
Starch-rich endodermis of dicot stems.
Large empty epidermal cells in grass leaves that let leaves roll in drought.
Cork cambium, which produces cork outside and phelloderm inside.

rd-school-c11-biology-a.ch07-structural-.title: Structural Organisation in Animals
rd-school-c11-biology-a.ch07-structural-.subtitle: Four kinds of tissue build every animal — and the frog shows how they become organs and systems
tags: Structural Organisation in Plants and Animals

sections.h: From a cell to a croaking frog
sections.md:
After the first heavy shower of the monsoon, the fields around Nashik suddenly fill with sound: frogs, hundreds of them, calling through the night. Each of those frogs began as a single fertilised egg. That one cell divided into trillions, and the cells did not stay alike. Some flattened into sheets that line the mouth; some stretched into fibres that contract; some grew long branching arms that carry electrical messages; some surrounded themselves with a hard mineral matrix and became bone.

In a single-celled organism like *Amoeba*, one cell does everything: digestion, respiration, excretion, movement. In multicellular animals, cells **divide the labour**. Groups of similar cells, together with the material between them, carry out a common function: a **tissue**. Tissues combine into **organs** (the stomach, the heart, the lungs). Organs work together as **organ systems** (the digestive system, the circulatory system). Organisation at each level gives rise to new abilities — a stomach can do what no individual cell can.

**cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organism**

In spite of the enormous variety of animals, all their tissues fall into just **four basic types**:

1. **Epithelial**
2. **Connective**
3. **Muscular**
4. **Neural**

In the second half of this read we will use the frog — a classic laboratory animal, now studied mostly through models and diagrams — to see how these tissues build real organ systems.

check.q: Which sequence correctly shows levels of organisation?
check.why: Similar cells form tissues, tissues form organs, and organs cooperate as organ systems.

sections.h: Epithelial tissue: the linings and coverings
sections.md:
**Epithelium** is the tissue that covers surfaces and lines cavities, ducts and tubes. Its cells are packed tightly with very little material between them, and they sit on a non-cellular **basement membrane**. One surface faces a body fluid or the outside world. There are two broad kinds: **simple** and **compound**.

**Simple epithelium** is a single layer of cells, found in linings of body cavities, ducts and tubes. By cell shape:

- **Squamous** — a single thin layer of flattened cells with irregular borders, like floor tiles. Found in the walls of blood vessels and the **air sacs of lungs**, where it allows easy diffusion. It forms a diffusion boundary.
- **Cuboidal** — a single layer of cube-like cells. Found in ducts of glands and tubular parts of **nephrons** in the kidney, mainly for secretion and absorption. In the proximal convoluted tubule, the cells bear **microvilli** to increase absorbing surface.
- **Columnar** — a single layer of tall, slender cells with nuclei near the base. Free surfaces may have microvilli. Found lining the stomach and intestine, helping in secretion and absorption. When columnar or cuboidal cells bear **cilia** on their free surface, they are **ciliated epithelium**; cilia move particles or mucus in a specific direction. Found in inner surfaces of hollow organs like bronchioles and fallopian tubes.

Some columnar or cuboidal cells become specialised for secretion: **glandular epithelium**. Glands are **unicellular** (isolated goblet cells of the alimentary canal) or **multicellular** (salivary gland). By how they release secretions, glands are **exocrine** — secreting mucus, saliva, earwax, oil, milk, digestive enzymes and other cell products through **ducts** — or **endocrine**, which have no ducts and release **hormones** directly into the fluid bathing the gland.

**Compound epithelium** is made of **more than one layer** (multi-layered) of cells, so its role in secretion and absorption is limited. Its main function is **protection against chemical and mechanical stresses**. It covers the dry surface of the skin, the moist surface of the buccal cavity and pharynx, the inner lining of ducts of salivary glands and of pancreatic ducts.

**Cell junctions.** All cells in epithelium are held together with little intercellular material. Three special junctions provide structural and functional links:

- **Tight junctions** stop substances from leaking across a tissue.
- **Adhering junctions** cement neighbouring cells together.
- **Gap junctions** connect the cytoplasm of adjoining cells, allowing rapid transfer of ions, small molecules and sometimes big molecules.

sections.md:
**Connective tissues** are the most abundant and widely distributed tissues in the bodies of complex animals. They link and support other tissues and organs, from soft to rigid: cartilage, bone, adipose tissue and blood are all connective tissues. In all of them except blood, the cells secrete fibres of structural proteins called **collagen** or **elastin**, which give strength, elasticity and flexibility. The cells also secrete modified polysaccharides that collect between cells and fibres as a **matrix** (ground substance).

**1. Loose connective tissue** has cells and fibres loosely arranged in a semi-fluid ground substance.

- **Areolar tissue** lies beneath the skin. It contains **fibroblasts** (cells that produce and secrete fibres), **macrophages** and **mast cells**, and serves as a support framework for epithelium.
- **Adipose tissue**, another loose connective tissue, lies mainly beneath the skin. Its cells are specialised to **store fats**. Excess nutrients not used immediately are converted into fats and stored here.

**2. Dense connective tissue** has fibres and fibroblasts compactly packed.

- In **dense regular** tissue, collagen fibres lie in rows between many parallel bundles of fibres. **Tendons**, which attach skeletal muscles to bones, and **ligaments**, which attach one bone to another, are examples.
- **Dense irregular** tissue has fibroblasts and many fibres, mostly collagen, oriented differently. It is present in the **skin**.

**3. Specialised connective tissue**: cartilage, bones and blood.

- **Cartilage** — the intercellular material is solid and pliable and resists compression. Cells (**chondrocytes**) are enclosed in small cavities within the matrix they secrete. Most cartilage in vertebrate embryos is replaced by bone in adults. Cartilage remains at the tip of the nose, the outer ear joints, between adjacent bones of the vertebral column, and in limbs and hands of adults.
- **Bone** — a hard, non-pliable ground substance rich in **calcium salts** and collagen fibres, giving strength. It is the main tissue providing the structural frame of the body. Bones support and protect softer tissues and organs. Bone cells (**osteocytes**) are present in spaces called **lacunae**. Limb bones like the long bones of the legs serve weight-bearing functions. They also interact with skeletal muscles attached to them to bring about movement. The **bone marrow** in some bones is the site of production of blood cells.
- **Blood** — a fluid connective tissue with plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets. It is the main circulating fluid that helps in transport of various substances. (You will study it in Body Fluids and Circulation.)
keyTerms: Fibroblast — cell that makes connective tissue fibres
Chondrocyte — cartilage cell in a lacuna
Osteocyte — bone cell in a lacuna
Collagen — strong structural protein fibre

check.q: Which connective tissue does NOT have fibres secreted by its cells?
check.why: Blood is a fluid connective tissue whose cells do not secrete collagen or elastin fibres.

sections.md:
Each muscle is made of many long, cylindrical **fibres** arranged in parallel arrays. These fibres are composed of numerous fine **myofibrils**. Muscle fibres **contract** (shorten) in response to stimulation, then **relax** (lengthen) and return to their uncontracted state in a coordinated fashion. Their action moves the body to adjust to changes in environment and also moves internal parts. In general, muscles play an active role in all movements of the body. There are three types:

**Skeletal muscle** is closely attached to skeletal bones. In a typical muscle such as the biceps, **striated (striped)** skeletal muscle fibres are bundled together in a parallel fashion. A sheath of tough connective tissue encloses several bundles of muscle fibres. Skeletal muscles are under **voluntary** control — you decide to lift your arm.

**Smooth muscle** fibres taper at both ends (fusiform) and **do not show striations**. Cell junctions hold them together and they are bundled together in a connective tissue sheath. The walls of internal organs such as blood vessels, stomach and intestine contain this type. Smooth muscles are **involuntary** — we usually cannot control their functioning; you cannot make your intestine move food faster just by willing it.

**Cardiac muscle** is a contractile tissue present **only in the heart**. Cell junctions fuse the plasma membranes of cardiac muscle cells and make them stick together. Communication junctions (**intercalated discs**) at some fusion points allow the cells to contract as a unit: when one cell receives a signal to contract, its neighbours are also stimulated. Cardiac muscle is **striated and involuntary**, and branched.

| Feature | Skeletal | Smooth | Cardiac |
|---|---|---|---|
| Striations | Present | Absent | Present |
| Shape | Long cylindrical, unbranched | Spindle-shaped | Branched |
| Nuclei | Many (multinucleate), peripheral | One, central | One (or two), central |
| Control | Voluntary | Involuntary | Involuntary |
| Location | Attached to bones | Walls of gut, vessels, iris | Heart |
| Special feature | Fast, can tire | Slow, sustained | Intercalated discs; never rests |

check.why: Intercalated discs link cardiac muscle cells so the heart contracts as a coordinated unit.

sections.md:
**Neural tissue** exerts the greatest control over the body's responsiveness to changing conditions. **Neurons**, the unit of the neural system, are **excitable cells**. The **neuroglial cells** that make up the rest of the neural system protect and support neurons. Neuroglia make up **more than one-half the volume** of neural tissue in our body.

When a neuron is suitably stimulated, an **electrical disturbance** is generated that swiftly travels along its plasma membrane. Arrival of the disturbance at the neuron's endings, or output zone, triggers events that may cause stimulation or inhibition of adjacent neurons and other cells.

A neuron has a **cell body** containing the nucleus, short branched **dendrites** that receive signals, and a long **axon** that carries signals away. You will meet the neuron in full detail, including how the impulse travels, in the chapter on Neural Control and Coordination.

**Did you know?** The longest cells in your body are neurons: a single motor neuron running from the base of the spinal cord to the big toe can be about a metre long.

check.q: Neuroglial cells:
options: Protect and support neurons and make up over half of neural tissue volume
check.why: Neuroglia are supporting cells that make up more than half the volume of neural tissue; neurons are the excitable cells.

sections.md:
Frogs live both on land and in fresh water and belong to class **Amphibia** of phylum Chordata. The most common species in India is ***Rana tigrina*** (the Indian bullfrog, now often placed in genus *Hoplobatrachus*).

Frogs do not have a constant body temperature: their body temperature varies with the environment. Such animals are **cold-blooded** or **poikilotherms**. Frogs can also change colour to hide from enemies — **camouflage** — a protective coloration called **mimicry** in some texts. Frogs are not seen during peak summer and winter: they take shelter in deep burrows to escape extreme heat and cold. This is **summer sleep (aestivation)** and **winter sleep (hibernation)**.

**Morphology.** The skin is smooth and slippery due to **mucus**. The skin is always kept moist. The colour of the dorsal side is generally olive green with dark irregular spots; on the ventral side the skin is uniformly pale yellow. The frog **never drinks water** but absorbs it through the skin.

The body is divisible into **head and trunk**; a **neck and tail are absent**. Above the mouth, a pair of **nostrils** is present. Eyes are bulged and covered by a **nictitating membrane** that protects them while in water. On either side of the eyes a membranous **tympanum** (ear) receives sound signals. Forelimbs and hindlimbs help in swimming, walking, leaping and burrowing. Hindlimbs end in **five digits** and are larger and more muscular than forelimbs, which end in **four digits**. Feet have **webbed digits** that help in swimming.

Frogs exhibit **sexual dimorphism**: male frogs can be distinguished by the presence of **sound-producing vocal sacs** and a **copulatory pad** on the first digit of the forelimbs, both absent in females.

sections.md:
The body cavity of the frog houses well-developed digestive, circulatory, respiratory, nervous, excretory and reproductive systems.

**Digestive system.** The alimentary canal is **short** because frogs are **carnivores**, so the intestine is reduced. The mouth opens into the buccal cavity, which leads through the pharynx to the oesophagus — a short tube opening into the stomach, which continues as the intestine, rectum and finally opens outside through the **cloaca**. The liver secretes **bile** stored in the gall bladder. The pancreas, a digestive gland, produces **pancreatic juice** with digestive enzymes. Food is captured by the **bilobed tongue**. Digestion is accomplished by the action of HCl and gastric juices in the stomach. Partially digested food (**chyme**) passes to the duodenum, which receives bile and pancreatic juice through a common bile duct. Bile emulsifies fat; pancreatic juice digests carbohydrates and proteins. Final digestion takes place in the intestine. Digested food is absorbed by the numerous finger-like folds in the inner wall of the intestine, the **villi** and **microvilli**. Undigested solid waste moves into the rectum and passes out through the cloaca.

**Respiration.** Frogs respire on land and in water by two different methods. In water, the skin acts as an aquatic respiratory organ (**cutaneous respiration**) — dissolved oxygen diffuses in through the skin. On land, the **buccal cavity, skin and lungs** act as respiratory organs; respiration by lungs is **pulmonary respiration**. The lungs are a pair of elongated, pink, sac-like structures in the upper part of the trunk region (thorax). Air enters through the nostrils into the buccal cavity and then to the lungs. During aestivation and hibernation, gaseous exchange takes place through the skin.

**Circulation.** The vascular system is well developed and **closed**. Frogs also have a **lymphatic system**. The blood vascular system involves heart, blood vessels and blood; the lymphatic system has lymph, lymph channels and lymph nodes. The heart is a muscular structure in the upper part of the body cavity with **three chambers: two atria and one ventricle**, covered by a membrane called the **pericardium**. A triangular structure, the **sinus venosus**, joins the right atrium and receives blood through the major veins called **vena cava**. The ventricle opens into a sac-like **conus arteriosus** on the ventral side of the heart. Blood from the heart is carried to all parts of the body by arteries (arterial system); veins collect blood from different parts back to the heart (venous system). Frogs have special venous connections between the liver and intestine and between the kidney and the lower parts of the body: the **hepatic portal system** and the **renal portal system**. Blood is composed of plasma and cells — RBCs (nucleated, containing the red pigment haemoglobin), WBCs and platelets. Lymph differs from blood: it lacks a few proteins and RBCs. Blood carries nutrients, gases and water to the respective sites.

**Excretion.** A well-developed system: a pair of **kidneys**, ureters, cloaca and urinary bladder. The kidneys are compact, dark red and bean-like, situated a little posteriorly in the body cavity on both sides of the vertebral column. Each kidney has several structural and functional units called **uriniferous tubules** or **nephrons**. Two ureters emerge from the kidneys in the male; in males the ureters act as a **urinogenital duct** opening into the cloaca. In females the ureters and oviduct open separately in the cloaca. The thin-walled urinary bladder lies ventral to the rectum and also opens into the cloaca. The frog excretes **urea** and is thus a **ureotelic** animal. Excretory wastes are carried by blood into the kidney, where they are separated and excreted.

**Control and coordination.** A highly evolved system of both **neural and endocrine** control. Important endocrine glands include the pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, thymus, pineal body, pancreatic islets, adrenals and gonads. The nervous system is organised into a **central nervous system** (brain and spinal cord), a **peripheral nervous system** (cranial and spinal nerves) and an **autonomic nervous system** (sympathetic and parasympathetic). There are **ten pairs of cranial nerves** arising from the brain. The brain is enclosed in a bony structure, the brain box (**cranium**), and is divided into **forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain**. The forebrain includes olfactory lobes, paired cerebral hemispheres and the unpaired diencephalon. The midbrain has a pair of **optic lobes**. The hindbrain consists of the cerebellum and medulla oblongata, which passes out through the foramen magnum and continues into the spinal cord, enclosed in the vertebral column. Sense organs include organs of touch (sensory papillae), taste (taste buds), smell (nasal epithelium), vision (eyes) and hearing (tympanum with internal ears). Eyes and internal ears are well-organised; the rest are cellular aggregations around nerve endings. Frogs have **simple eyes** (one unit).

**Reproduction.** Male reproductive organs: a pair of yellowish ovoid **testes** adhered to the upper part of the kidneys by a double fold of peritoneum called **mesorchium**. **Vasa efferentia**, 10–12 in number, arise from the testes, enter the kidneys on their side and open into the **Bidder's canal**, which finally communicates with the urinogenital duct that comes out of the kidneys and opens into the cloaca. The cloaca is a small median chamber used to pass faecal matter, urine and sperms to the exterior. Female organs: a pair of **ovaries**, situated near the kidneys with no functional connection to them. A pair of oviducts arising from the ovaries opens into the cloaca separately. A mature female can lay **2500 to 3000 ova** at a time. **Fertilisation is external** and takes place in water. Development involves a larval stage called the **tadpole**, which undergoes **metamorphosis** to form the adult.

**Frogs and us.** Frogs are beneficial: they eat insects and protect crops. They maintain ecological balance as an important link in food chains and food webs. In some countries the muscular legs of frogs are used as food. Over-collection of frogs has harmed wild populations in several regions, so frogs are protected in many places — including India, which banned the export of frog legs in 1987.

check.why: Frogs convert nitrogenous waste mainly into urea, so they are ureotelic.

summary: Cells with a common function form tissues; tissues form organs and organ systems.
Four basic animal tissues: epithelial, connective, muscular and neural.
Simple epithelia: squamous (lung air sacs, vessels), cuboidal (nephron tubules), columnar (gut lining), ciliated (bronchioles, fallopian tubes).
Compound epithelium is multi-layered and protective (skin, buccal cavity).
Glands are exocrine (ducts) or endocrine (no ducts, hormones).
Tight junctions seal, adhering junctions cement, gap junctions connect cytoplasm.
Connective tissues: loose (areolar, adipose), dense (tendons, ligaments, skin), specialised (cartilage, bone, blood).
Muscles: skeletal (striated, voluntary), smooth (unstriated, involuntary), cardiac (striated, involuntary, intercalated discs).
Neural tissue: excitable neurons plus neuroglia (over half the volume).
Frogs are poikilotherms; they aestivate and hibernate, absorb water through skin and show sexual dimorphism.
Frog respiration is cutaneous in water and pulmonary plus buccal on land.
Frog heart has three chambers with sinus venosus and conus arteriosus; hepatic and renal portal systems exist.
Frogs are ureotelic; males have a urinogenital duct; fertilisation is external and development includes a tadpole and metamorphosis.
Frog brain: forebrain, midbrain (optic lobes), hindbrain; ten pairs of cranial nerves.

sections.h: What is a cell — and how did we find out?
sections.md:
Prick your finger and look at a drop of blood under a good microscope: thousands of tiny red discs drift past. Scrape the inside of your cheek with a toothpick, stain it, and you see flat cells with dark dots in the middle. Peel the thin skin from an onion scale and you see a neat brick wall of rectangular boxes. Every living thing you know is made of these units.

The word **cell** was first used by **Robert Hooke** in 1665, looking at thin slices of cork: the empty, box-like compartments reminded him of monks' small rooms. What he saw were dead cell walls. **Anton van Leeuwenhoek** first saw and described a **live cell**. **Robert Brown** later discovered the **nucleus**. With better microscopes and, much later, the **electron microscope**, the fine structure of cells was revealed.

**Cell theory.** In **1838**, the German botanist **Matthias Schleiden** examined many plants and concluded that all plants are composed of different kinds of cells which form tissues. At about the same time, in **1839**, the British zoologist **Theodore Schwann** studied different animal cells and reported that cells had a thin outer layer — today's plasma membrane. He also concluded, from plant tissues, that the **cell wall** is unique to plant cells. Schwann proposed that the bodies of animals and plants are composed of cells and products of cells. Together they formulated the **cell theory**. But it did not explain how new cells form. In **1855**, **Rudolf Virchow** explained that cells divide and new cells are formed from pre-existing cells: ***Omnis cellula-e cellula***. He modified the hypothesis to give the cell theory a final shape:

1. all living organisms are composed of cells and products of cells;
2. all cells arise from pre-existing cells.

Anything less than a complete cell does not ensure independent living. Hence the cell is the **fundamental structural and functional unit of all living organisms**.

items.what: Schleiden: plants are made of cells
Schwann: animals too; cell wall unique to plants

check.why: Virchow (1855) completed the cell theory with 'Omnis cellula-e cellula'.

sections.h: An overview: prokaryotes, eukaryotes and sizes
sections.md:
Onion cells, a typical plant cell, have a distinct **cell wall** as the outer boundary and just within it the **cell membrane**. Human cheek cells have an outer membrane as the delimiting structure but no cell wall. Inside every cell lies a dense membrane-bound structure, the **nucleus**, containing **chromosomes** that carry the genetic material **DNA**. Cells with a membrane-bound nucleus are **eukaryotic**; those without are **prokaryotic**. In both, a semi-fluid matrix called **cytoplasm** occupies the volume of the cell. It is the main arena of cellular activities.

Eukaryotic cells have distinct **membrane-bound organelles** — endoplasmic reticulum (ER), Golgi complex, lysosomes, mitochondria, microbodies and vacuoles. Prokaryotes lack these. **Ribosomes** are non-membrane-bound organelles found in all cells — both in the cytoplasm and within chloroplasts (in plants) and mitochondria, and on rough ER. Animal cells contain another non-membrane-bound organelle, the **centrosome**, which helps in cell division.

**Size and shape vary enormously.** *Mycoplasma*, the smallest cells, are only about **0.3 µm** long; bacteria are 3–5 µm. The largest isolated single cell is the **egg of an ostrich**. Among multicellular organisms, human red blood cells are about **7.0 µm** in diameter. **Nerve cells** are some of the longest. Shapes vary with function: disc-like (RBCs), polygonal, columnar, cuboid, thread-like, or even irregular (amoeba).

| Feature | Prokaryotic cell | Eukaryotic cell |
|---|---|---|
| Nucleus | No nuclear membrane; nucleoid | True nucleus with envelope |
| Membrane-bound organelles | Absent | Present |
| Ribosomes | 70S | 80S in cytoplasm (70S in mitochondria, chloroplasts) |
| DNA | Single circular, plus plasmids | Several linear chromosomes |
| Examples | Bacteria, cyanobacteria, mycoplasma | Protists, fungi, plants, animals |

*1 µm (micrometre) = one-thousandth of a millimetre = 10⁻⁶ m.*

check.q: Which organelle is found in BOTH prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
check.why: Ribosomes are non-membrane-bound and present in all cells; the others are membrane-bound eukaryotic organelles.

sections.md:
Prokaryotic cells are represented by **bacteria, blue-green algae, mycoplasma** and **PPLO** (pleuro-pneumonia-like organisms). They are generally smaller and multiply more rapidly than eukaryotic cells. Their four basic shapes are bacillus (rod), coccus (spherical), vibrio (comma) and spirillum (spiral).

All prokaryotes have a **cell wall** surrounding the cell membrane, **except mycoplasma**. The fluid matrix filling the cell is the cytoplasm. There is no well-defined nucleus; the genetic material is basically **naked**, not enveloped by a nuclear membrane. In addition to genomic DNA (the single chromosome, a circular DNA), many bacteria have small circular DNA outside the genomic DNA, called **plasmids**. Plasmids confer certain unique phenotypic characters — such as **resistance to antibiotics**. In higher classes you will learn that plasmid DNA is used to monitor bacterial transformation with foreign DNA. A specialised differentiated form of cell membrane, the **mesosome**, is a characteristic of prokaryotes.

**Cell envelope.** Most prokaryotic cells, particularly bacteria, have a chemically complex envelope with a tightly bound **three-layered** structure: the outermost **glycocalyx**, followed by the **cell wall** and the **plasma membrane**. Each layer has a distinct function, but together they act as a single protective unit. Based on differences in the envelope and their response to a staining procedure developed by Gram, bacteria are **Gram positive** (take up the stain) or **Gram negative** (do not).

The glycocalyx differs: it could be a loose sheath called the **slime layer**, or thick and tough, called the **capsule**. The cell wall determines shape and gives strong structural support to prevent the bacterium from bursting or collapsing. The plasma membrane is semi-permeable and structurally similar to that of eukaryotes.

**Mesosomes** are formed by extensions of the plasma membrane into the cell — vesicles, tubules and lamellae. They help in cell wall formation, DNA replication and distribution to daughter cells, respiration, secretion processes, and increase the surface area of the plasma membrane and enzymatic content. In some prokaryotes such as cyanobacteria, other membranous extensions into the cytoplasm, **chromatophores**, contain pigments.

Bacterial cells may be motile or non-motile. If motile, they have thin filamentous extensions, **flagella**. A bacterial flagellum has three parts: **filament, hook and basal body**. Besides flagella, **pili** and **fimbriae** are surface structures that do not play a role in motility. Pili are elongated tubular structures made of a special protein. Fimbriae are small bristle-like fibres sprouting out; in some bacteria they help attach to rocks in streams and to host tissues.

**Ribosomes and inclusion bodies.** In prokaryotes, ribosomes are associated with the plasma membrane. They are about 15 nm by 20 nm, made of two subunits — **50S and 30S** — that together form **70S** prokaryotic ribosomes. Ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis. Several ribosomes may attach to a single mRNA to form a chain called **polyribosome** or **polysome**. Reserve material in prokaryotes is stored in the cytoplasm as **inclusion bodies**, not bounded by membranes, lying free: phosphate granules, cyanophycean granules and glycogen granules. **Gas vacuoles** are found in blue-green and purple and green photosynthetic bacteria.
