sections.h: The cell membrane: a fluid mosaic
sections.md:
The detailed structure of the membrane was studied only after the electron microscope arrived in the 1950s. Chemical studies, especially of human red blood cells (RBCs), showed that the cell membrane is mainly composed of **lipids and proteins**. The major lipids are **phospholipids** arranged in a **bilayer**. The lipids are arranged with their **polar heads towards the outer sides** and **hydrophobic tails towards the inner part**. This ensures the non-polar tails of saturated hydrocarbons are protected from the aqueous environment. The membrane also contains **cholesterol**.

Biochemical investigation showed membranes also possess protein and carbohydrate. The ratio of protein to lipid varies in different cell types. In human RBCs, the membrane has about **52% protein and 40% lipids**. Depending on how easily they can be extracted, membrane proteins are **integral** (partially or totally buried in the membrane) or **peripheral** (lying on the surface).

An improved model, widely accepted, is the **fluid mosaic model** proposed by **Singer and Nicolson (1972)**. According to it, the quasi-fluid nature of the lipid enables lateral movement of proteins within the overall bilayer. This ability to move within the membrane is measured as its **fluidity**. Fluidity is important for functions like **cell growth, formation of intercellular junctions, secretion, endocytosis and cell division**.

One of the most important functions of the plasma membrane is **transport** of molecules across it. The membrane is **selectively permeable** to some molecules present on either side. Many molecules can move briefly across the membrane without any energy requirement: **passive transport**. Neutral solutes move by **simple diffusion** along the concentration gradient — from higher to lower concentration. Water may also move by diffusion across the membrane: **osmosis**. Polar molecules cannot pass through the non-polar lipid bilayer and need a **carrier protein**. A few ions or molecules are transported against their concentration gradient — from lower to higher — which requires energy from ATP: **active transport**, e.g. the **Na⁺/K⁺ pump**.

sections.h: Cell wall and the endomembrane system
sections.md:
A non-living rigid structure, the **cell wall**, forms an outer covering for the plasma membrane of fungi and plants. It gives shape, protects from mechanical damage and infection, helps cell-to-cell interaction and acts as a barrier to undesirable macromolecules. Algae have walls of **cellulose, galactans, mannans** and minerals like **calcium carbonate**; other plants have **cellulose, hemicellulose, pectins and proteins**. The wall of a young plant cell, the **primary wall**, can grow; it gradually diminishes as the cell matures and a **secondary wall** forms on the inner (membrane-facing) side. The **middle lamella** is a layer mainly of **calcium pectate** that holds or glues neighbouring cells together. The wall and middle lamellae may be traversed by **plasmodesmata**, connecting the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells.

**The endomembrane system.** While each membranous organelle is distinct in structure and function, many are considered together because their functions are coordinated: **ER, Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles**. Mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes are not part of it since their functions are not coordinated with these.

**Endoplasmic reticulum (ER).** Electron microscopy revealed a network of tiny tubular structures scattered in the cytoplasm. The ER divides the intracellular space into two compartments — **luminal** (inside ER) and **extra-luminal** (cytoplasm). ER often bears ribosomes on its outer surface: **rough ER (RER)**; without ribosomes it appears smooth: **smooth ER (SER)**. RER is frequently observed in cells actively involved in **protein synthesis and secretion**; it is extensive and continuous with the outer membrane of the nucleus. SER is the major site for synthesis of **lipids**. In animal cells, lipid-like **steroidal hormones** are synthesised in SER.

**Golgi apparatus.** Camillo **Golgi (1898)** first observed densely stained reticular structures near the nucleus, later named Golgi bodies after him. They consist of many flat, disc-shaped sacs or **cisternae**, 0.5–1.0 µm in diameter, stacked parallel to each other. The Golgi cisternae are concentrically arranged near the nucleus with distinct convex **cis** (forming) face and concave **trans** (maturing) face. The cis and trans faces are entirely different but interconnected. The Golgi apparatus principally **packages materials** to be delivered either to intracellular targets or secreted outside the cell. Materials to be packaged, in the form of vesicles from the ER, fuse with the cis face and move towards the maturing face. This explains why the Golgi apparatus remains in close association with the ER. A number of proteins synthesised by ribosomes on the ER are modified in the Golgi cisternae before release from the trans face. The Golgi apparatus is the important site of formation of **glycoproteins and glycolipids**.

**Lysosomes** are membrane-bound vesicular structures formed by packaging in the Golgi apparatus. Isolated lysosomal vesicles are very rich in almost all types of **hydrolytic enzymes** (hydrolases — lipases, proteases, carbohydrases) **optimally active at acidic pH**. These enzymes can digest carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids.

**Vacuoles** are membrane-bound spaces found in the cytoplasm, containing water, sap, excretory products and other materials not useful for the cell. The vacuole is bound by a single membrane called the **tonoplast**. In plant cells vacuoles can occupy up to **90 per cent** of the cell's volume. In plants, the tonoplast facilitates transport of a number of ions and other materials against concentration gradients into the vacuole, so their concentration is significantly higher in the vacuole than in the cytoplasm. In *Amoeba*, the **contractile vacuole** is important for osmoregulation and excretion. In many cells, as in protists, **food vacuoles** form by engulfing food particles.

sections.h: Mitochondria, plastids, ribosomes and the cytoskeleton
sections.md:
**Mitochondria** are not easily visible under a light microscope unless specifically stained. Their number per cell varies widely depending on its physiological activity. They are typically sausage-shaped or cylindrical, about 0.2–1.0 µm (average 0.5 µm) in diameter and 1.0–4.1 µm long. Each mitochondrion is a **double-membrane-bound** structure: the outer and inner membranes divide its lumen into two aqueous compartments — the outer compartment and the inner compartment, which is filled with a dense homogeneous substance, the **matrix**. The outer membrane forms the continuous limiting boundary. The inner membrane forms a number of infoldings called **cristae** towards the matrix, which increase surface area. Each membrane has its own specific enzymes associated with mitochondrial function. Mitochondria are the sites of **aerobic respiration** and produce cellular energy as **ATP** — hence the '**power houses**' of the cell. The matrix also possesses a **single circular DNA**, a few RNA molecules, **70S ribosomes** and components required for protein synthesis. Mitochondria divide by **fission**.

**Plastids** are found in all plant cells and in euglenoides. They are easily observed under the microscope as they are large, and bear specific pigments, giving plants specific colours. By pigment type, plastids are **chloroplasts, chromoplasts and leucoplasts**.

- **Chloroplasts** contain chlorophyll and carotenoid pigments, which trap light energy for photosynthesis.
- **Chromoplasts** contain fat-soluble carotenoid pigments like carotene and xanthophylls, giving yellow, orange or red colour (ripe tomato, carrot, chilli).
- **Leucoplasts** are colourless plastids of varied shapes and sizes with stored nutrients: **amyloplasts** store starch (potato), **elaioplasts** store oils and fats, and **aleuroplasts** store proteins.

Majority of chloroplasts of green plants are in the mesophyll cells of leaves. They are lens-shaped, oval, spherical, discoid or even ribbon-like, 5–10 µm long and 2–4 µm wide. Their number varies from one per cell in *Chlamydomonas* to 20–40 per cell in the mesophyll. Like mitochondria, chloroplasts are **double membrane-bound**. Of the two, the inner membrane is relatively less permeable. The space limited by the inner membrane is the **stroma**. A number of organised flattened membranous sacs called **thylakoids** are present in the stroma. Thylakoids are arranged in stacks like piles of coins called **grana** (singular granum), or the intergranal thylakoids. In addition, flat membranous tubules called **stroma lamellae** connect the thylakoids of different grana. The membrane of the thylakoids encloses a space called the **lumen**. The stroma contains enzymes required for synthesis of carbohydrates and proteins, plus small double-stranded circular DNA and ribosomes. Chlorophyll pigments are present in the thylakoids. The ribosomes of chloroplasts are smaller (**70S**) than cytoplasmic ribosomes (**80S**).

**Ribosomes** are granular structures first observed under the electron microscope as dense particles by **George Palade (1953)**. They are composed of RNA and proteins and are **not surrounded by any membrane**. Eukaryotic ribosomes are 80S, prokaryotic 70S. Here 'S' (**Svedberg unit**) stands for the sedimentation coefficient; it indirectly measures density and size. Both 70S and 80S ribosomes are composed of two subunits (60S + 40S in eukaryotes; 50S + 30S in prokaryotes).

**Cytoskeleton.** An elaborate network of filamentous proteinaceous structures in the cytoplasm — **microtubules, microfilaments and intermediate filaments** — involved in mechanical support, motility, and maintenance of the shape of the cell.

**Cilia and flagella.** Cilia (singular cilium) and flagella are hair-like outgrowths of the cell membrane. Cilia are small structures that work like **oars**, causing movement of either the cell or the surrounding fluid. Flagella are comparatively longer and responsible for cell movement. Prokaryotic bacteria also possess flagella, but these are **structurally different** from eukaryotic flagella. Under the electron microscope, a cilium or flagellum is covered with plasma membrane. Its core, the **axoneme**, has a number of microtubules running parallel to the long axis: **nine pairs of doublets of radially arranged peripheral microtubules and a pair of centrally located microtubules** — the **9+2 array**. The central tubules are connected by bridges and enclosed by a central sheath, which is connected to one of the tubules of each peripheral doublet by a radial spoke. The peripheral doublets are interconnected by linkers. Both cilium and flagellum emerge from centriole-like structures called **basal bodies**.

**Centrosome and centrioles.** The centrosome is an organelle usually containing two cylindrical structures called **centrioles**, surrounded by amorphous **pericentriolar materials**. Both centrioles lie **perpendicular** to each other, each with an organisation like a cartwheel. They are made up of **nine evenly spaced peripheral fibrils of tubulin protein**; each peripheral fibril is a **triplet**. Adjacent triplets are linked. The central part of the proximal region of the centriole is also proteinaceous and called the **hub**, connected to tubules of the peripheral triplets by radial spokes. Centrioles form the basal body of cilia or flagella, and **spindle fibres** that give rise to the spindle apparatus during cell division in animal cells.

sections.md:
The **nucleus** as a cell organelle was first described by **Robert Brown** as early as **1831**. Later the material of the nucleus stained by basic dyes was given the name **chromatin** by **Flemming**.

The interphase nucleus (a nucleus of a cell not dividing) has highly extended and elaborate nucleoprotein fibres called **chromatin**, a nuclear matrix, and one or more spherical bodies called **nucleoli** (singular nucleolus). Electron microscopy has revealed that the **nuclear envelope**, with two parallel membranes and a space between them (the **perinuclear space**) of 10–50 nm, forms a barrier between the materials inside the nucleus and the cytoplasm. The outer membrane usually remains continuous with the ER and bears ribosomes. At a number of places the nuclear envelope is interrupted by minute **pores**, formed by the fusion of its two membranes. These pores are the passages through which movement of RNA and protein molecules takes place in both directions between nucleus and cytoplasm. Normally there is only one nucleus per cell, though variations exist: some mature cells even lack a nucleus — **erythrocytes of many mammals** and **sieve tube cells** of vascular plants. Would you consider these cells 'living'?

The nuclear matrix or **nucleoplasm** contains the nucleolus and chromatin. Nucleoli are spherical structures in the nucleoplasm; their content is continuous with the rest of the nucleoplasm since the nucleolus is **not membrane-bound**. It is a site for active **ribosomal RNA synthesis**. Larger and more numerous nucleoli are present in cells actively carrying out protein synthesis.

During different stages of cell division, cells show structured **chromosomes** in place of the nucleus. Chromatin contains DNA and some basic proteins called **histones**, some non-histone proteins and also RNA. A single human cell has approximately **two metre long thread of DNA** distributed among its **46 chromosomes (23 pairs)**.

Every chromosome has a primary constriction, the **centromere**, on whose sides disc-shaped structures called **kinetochores** are present. Based on the position of the centromere, chromosomes are classified into four types:

- **Metacentric** — middle centromere forming two equal arms.
- **Sub-metacentric** — centromere nearer one end, one shorter arm and one longer arm.
- **Acrocentric** — centromere close to its end, forming one extremely short and one very long arm.
- **Telocentric** — a terminal centromere.

Sometimes a few chromosomes have non-staining secondary constrictions at a constant location, giving the appearance of a small fragment called the **satellite**.

**Microbodies.** Many membrane-bound minute vesicles called microbodies, containing various enzymes, are present in both plant and animal cells (peroxisomes and glyoxysomes, for example).

> The cell is not a bag of chemicals. It is a city with zoning laws: every reaction has its address.

summary: Cell theory: Schleiden (1838) and Schwann (1839); Virchow (1855) added that cells arise from pre-existing cells.
Prokaryotes lack a nuclear membrane and membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotes have both.
Mycoplasma (about 0.3 µm) are the smallest cells; ostrich egg the largest single cell.
Bacterial envelope: glycocalyx, cell wall, plasma membrane; Gram positive vs Gram negative.
Mesosomes help wall formation, DNA replication, respiration; plasmids carry extra traits.
Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S (50S + 30S); eukaryotic 80S (60S + 40S).
Plasma membrane: lipid bilayer with proteins — fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972).
Passive transport: diffusion and osmosis; active transport uses ATP (Na⁺/K⁺ pump).
Plant cell wall: primary and secondary walls, middle lamella of calcium pectate, plasmodesmata.
Endomembrane system: ER, Golgi, lysosomes, vacuoles; RER makes proteins, SER lipids and steroids.
Golgi packages materials, forming glycoproteins and glycolipids; lysosomes hold acid hydrolases.
Mitochondria and chloroplasts are double-membraned with their own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes.
Cilia and flagella have a 9+2 axoneme; centrioles have nine triplets in a cartwheel.
Nucleus: double envelope with pores, nucleolus (rRNA synthesis), chromatin with DNA and histones.
Chromosomes are metacentric, sub-metacentric, acrocentric or telocentric by centromere position.

rd-school-c11-biology-b.ch19-chemical-co.title: Chemical Coordination and Integration
rd-school-c11-biology-b.ch19-chemical-co.subtitle: How tiny drops of hormone run your growth, your mood, your sugar and your sleep

sections.md:
It is the last over of an India–Pakistan match. Bumrah runs in, and in the stands you feel your heart thump, your palms go damp, your breath quicken. No nerve was told by you to do this. Within seconds a few millionths of a gram of a chemical, **adrenaline**, poured out of two small glands sitting on top of your kidneys and travelled in the blood to almost every organ.

That is **chemical coordination**. In the previous chapter you studied the nervous system, which coordinates the body with fast electrical impulses running along neurons — point-to-point, like a phone call. But neurons do not reach every cell, and their effects are short-lived. Many functions — growth over years, the steady level of blood sugar, the menstrual cycle, the rate at which every cell burns fuel — need slower, longer-lasting, body-wide control. That job belongs to **hormones**, made by the **endocrine system**.

| Feature | Neural coordination | Chemical (hormonal) coordination |
|---|---|---|
| Signal | Electrical impulse + neurotransmitter | Hormone carried in blood |
| Speed | Milliseconds | Seconds to days |
| Reach | Only cells a neuron touches | Any cell with the right receptor |
| Duration | Brief | Often long-lasting |

The two systems are not rivals. They work together, and the hypothalamus — part of the brain — is the bridge between them. Together they **integrate** the body so that it behaves as one organism.

> Did you know? The word *hormone* comes from a Greek word meaning 'to set in motion'. It was coined in 1905 by the British physiologist Ernest Starling.
keyTerms: Coordination — making organs work together in harmony
Integration — combining many signals into one coherent response

check.q: Which statement best contrasts hormonal with neural coordination?
options: Hormones act faster and more locally
Hormones act more slowly but can reach every cell that has a receptor
check.why: Hormones travel through the blood, so they are slower than nerve impulses but can reach any target cell bearing a matching receptor, often with long-lasting effects.

sections.md:
**Endocrine glands** are ductless: they lack ducts and release their secretions straight into the blood or the fluid around cells. This separates them from **exocrine glands** such as salivary or sweat glands, which pour their products through ducts.

The classical definition of a hormone was 'a chemical produced by an endocrine gland, released into the blood and carried to a distant target organ'. Modern biology widened it: a **hormone is a non-nutrient chemical that acts as an intercellular messenger and is produced in trace amounts**. This new definition includes chemicals made by scattered cells in the stomach, intestine, heart and kidney, which are not organised into glands at all.

Key features of hormones:
- They are made in **very small quantities** (nanograms to micrograms per day).
- They act only on **target cells** that carry specific **receptors**.
- They are not used as food or as building material — they carry *information*.
- They are destroyed or excreted after use, so their levels can be adjusted.

Invertebrates such as insects have simple endocrine systems with a few hormones (for example, moulting hormones). Vertebrates have many glands and dozens of hormones. In humans the main endocrine glands are the **pituitary, pineal, thyroid, adrenal, pancreas, parathyroid, thymus and gonads** (testes in males, ovaries in females). In addition, the **hypothalamus**, gastrointestinal tract, liver, kidney and heart produce hormones.

check.q: Why does the modern definition of hormone include chemicals from the stomach and heart?
options: Because a hormone is now defined as a trace non-nutrient intercellular messenger, wherever it is made
Because they act only locally as enzymes
check.why: The modern definition focuses on function — a non-nutrient chemical messenger made in trace amounts — so scattered secretory cells in many organs qualify even though they are not glands.

sections.h: The hypothalamus — the brain's command post
sections.md:
At the base of the forebrain lies the **hypothalamus**, a small region containing groups of neurosecretory cells called **nuclei**. These neurons do something unusual: instead of only firing impulses, they *secrete hormones*. This is where the nervous system hands over to the endocrine system.

Hypothalamic hormones are of two kinds:
- **Releasing hormones** stimulate the pituitary. Example: **GnRH** (gonadotrophin releasing hormone) stimulates the pituitary to make gonadotrophins; TRH stimulates TSH release; CRH stimulates ACTH release.
- **Inhibiting hormones** stop pituitary secretion. Example: **somatostatin** inhibits the release of growth hormone.

How do these reach the pituitary? Through a special set of blood vessels, the **hypophyseal portal system**, which carries them from the hypothalamus straight to the **anterior pituitary**. The **posterior pituitary**, on the other hand, is directly connected by nerve axons — the hypothalamic neurons extend down into it, and the hormones they make (oxytocin and vasopressin) travel down these axons to be stored and released there.

Think of the hypothalamus as the Prime Minister's Office: it rarely deals with citizens directly, but sends instructions to the ministries (pituitary), which then direct the state governments (thyroid, adrenal, gonads).

Hypophyseal portal system — blood vessels linking hypothalamus to anterior pituitary

check.q: Somatostatin from the hypothalamus is an example of a:
options: Inhibiting hormone that blocks growth hormone release
check.why: Somatostatin is a hypothalamic inhibiting hormone; it suppresses the release of growth hormone from the anterior pituitary.

sections.h: The pituitary — the 'master' that takes orders
sections.md:
The **pituitary gland** sits in a bony pocket called the **sella turcica** and hangs from the hypothalamus by a stalk. It is divided anatomically into the **adenohypophysis** and the **neurohypophysis**.

**Adenohypophysis** has two parts: the **pars distalis** (often called the anterior pituitary) and the **pars intermedia**. The pars distalis secretes six hormones:
1. **Growth hormone (GH)** — growth of the body. Too much GH in childhood causes **gigantism**; too little causes **pituitary dwarfism** (stunted growth). Excess GH in adults, especially in middle age, causes **acromegaly** — enlarged, disfigured face, hands and feet, which can be serious if not diagnosed early.
2. **Prolactin (PRL)** — growth of mammary glands and milk production.
3. **Thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH)** — makes the thyroid secrete its hormones.
4. **Adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH)** — makes the adrenal cortex secrete glucocorticoids.
5. **Luteinising hormone (LH)** and 6. **Follicle stimulating hormone (FSH)** — together called **gonadotrophins**. In males, LH stimulates the testes to make androgens; FSH with androgens regulates spermatogenesis. In females, LH induces ovulation of fully mature follicles (Graafian follicles) and maintains the corpus luteum; FSH stimulates growth and development of ovarian follicles.

The **pars intermedia** secretes **melanocyte stimulating hormone (MSH)**, which acts on melanocytes and regulates skin pigmentation. In humans the pars intermedia is almost merged with the pars distalis.

**Neurohypophysis (pars nervosa / posterior pituitary)** stores and releases two hormones that are actually *made in the hypothalamus*:
- **Oxytocin** — contraction of smooth muscles; strong uterine contractions during childbirth and milk ejection from the mammary glands.
- **Vasopressin (ADH, antidiuretic hormone)** — acts on the kidney's distal tubules to reabsorb water and electrolytes, reducing water loss in urine. Lack of ADH causes **diabetes insipidus**: the kidney cannot conserve water, so large volumes of dilute urine are passed and the person becomes dehydrated and very thirsty.

check.q: A patient passes very large volumes of dilute urine and is always thirsty, but blood sugar is normal. The most likely hormone deficiency is:
check.why: Without ADH the distal tubules cannot reabsorb water, causing diabetes insipidus — copious dilute urine with normal blood glucose.

sections.md:
**The pineal gland** lies on the dorsal side of the forebrain. It secretes **melatonin**, which plays a very important role in regulating our **24-hour (diurnal) rhythm** — the sleep–wake cycle and body temperature. Melatonin also influences metabolism, pigmentation, the menstrual cycle and defence capability. Melatonin release rises in darkness, which is why bright phone screens late at night can make it harder to fall asleep.

**The thyroid gland** has two lobes on either side of the trachea, joined by a thin flap called the **isthmus**. It is made of **follicles** and stromal tissue; each follicle is a ring of cells enclosing a cavity. The follicular cells make two hormones, **tetraiodothyronine (thyroxine, T₄)** and **triiodothyronine (T₃)**. As their names say, they contain iodine — iodine is essential for their normal synthesis.

Disorders:
- **Iodine deficiency** → **hypothyroidism** and enlargement of the gland, called **goitre**. India's use of iodised salt has greatly reduced goitre.
- Hypothyroidism during pregnancy can cause defective development of the baby, leading to stunted growth (**cretinism**), mental retardation, low intelligence quotient, abnormal skin and deaf-mutism. In adult women it may cause an irregular menstrual cycle.
- **Hyperthyroidism** (too much hormone, e.g. from a nodule or cancer) adversely affects body physiology. **Exophthalmic goitre (Graves' disease)** is a form of hyperthyroidism marked by an enlarged thyroid, protruding eyeballs, raised basal metabolic rate and weight loss.

Thyroid hormones regulate the **basal metabolic rate**, support red blood cell formation, control metabolism of carbohydrates, proteins and fats, and help maintain water and electrolyte balance. The thyroid also secretes a protein hormone, **thyrocalcitonin (TCT)**, which *lowers* blood calcium.

**The parathyroid glands** are four small glands on the back of the thyroid, one pair in each lobe. They secrete **parathyroid hormone (PTH)**, a peptide that *raises* blood Ca²⁺. PTH stimulates bone resorption (dissolving bone to release calcium), increases Ca²⁺ reabsorption by kidney tubules and increases Ca²⁺ absorption from digested food. PTH is therefore a **hypercalcemic** hormone, and with TCT it keeps calcium balanced — like two hands on a see-saw.

keyTerms: Goitre — enlarged thyroid, often from iodine deficiency
Hypercalcemic — raising blood calcium

check.q: Which pair of hormones has antagonistic effects on blood calcium?
check.why: PTH raises blood calcium by bone resorption and greater reabsorption, while thyrocalcitonin lowers it, so they balance each other.

sections.md:
**The thymus** is a lobular structure between the lungs, behind the sternum, on the ventral side of the aorta. It plays a major role in **immunity**. It secretes peptide hormones called **thymosins**, which help **T-lymphocytes** differentiate — these provide cell-mediated immunity. Thymosins also promote antibody production, aiding humoral immunity. The thymus is large in children and **degenerates in old age**, which partly explains why immune responses weaken in elderly people.

**The adrenal glands** — one pair, one on the anterior part of each kidney — each have two very different tissues: the outer **adrenal cortex** and the central **adrenal medulla**.

**Adrenal medulla** secretes **adrenaline (epinephrine)** and **noradrenaline (norepinephrine)**, together called **catecholamines**. They are released rapidly in response to stress and emergencies, so they are called **emergency hormones** or hormones of **Fight or Flight**. Effects: increased alertness, dilated pupils, raised hair (piloerection), sweating, faster heartbeat and stronger contraction, faster breathing, and breakdown of glycogen to glucose (raising blood sugar), plus breakdown of lipids and proteins.

**Adrenal cortex** has three layers, from outside in: **zona glomerulosa, zona fasciculata, zona reticularis**. Its hormones are **corticoids**:
- **Glucocorticoids** (mainly **cortisol**) — involved in carbohydrate metabolism: stimulate gluconeogenesis, lipolysis and proteolysis, and inhibit cellular uptake and use of amino acids. Cortisol maintains the cardiovascular system and kidney function, produces **anti-inflammatory** reactions, suppresses the immune response, and stimulates RBC production.
- **Mineralocorticoids** (mainly **aldosterone**) — act on renal tubules to reabsorb Na⁺ and water and excrete K⁺ and phosphate. This maintains electrolytes, body fluid volume, osmotic pressure and blood pressure.
- Small amounts of **androgenic steroids**, which play a role in the growth of axial, pubic and facial hair during puberty.

Underproduction of adrenal cortex hormones changes carbohydrate metabolism and causes acute weakness and fatigue — **Addison's disease**.

check.q: A deficiency of aldosterone would most directly lead to:
options: Loss of Na⁺ and water in urine, lowering blood volume and pressure
check.why: Aldosterone makes kidney tubules reabsorb Na⁺ and water; without it sodium and water are lost, so fluid volume and blood pressure fall.

sections.md:
The **pancreas** is a **composite gland**: it is both exocrine (digestive enzymes through the pancreatic duct) and endocrine. The endocrine part is made of about **1 to 2 million islets of Langerhans**, which form only **1–2 per cent** of pancreatic tissue. Each islet has mainly **α-cells**, which secrete **glucagon**, and **β-cells**, which secrete **insulin**.

**Glucagon** is a peptide hormone that keeps blood glucose from falling too low. It acts mainly on liver cells (hepatocytes), stimulating **glycogenolysis** (glycogen → glucose) and **gluconeogenesis** (new glucose from non-carbohydrates), so blood glucose rises — **hyperglycemia**. Glucagon also reduces cellular glucose uptake and use. So glucagon is a **hyperglycemic hormone**.

**Insulin** is a peptide hormone with the opposite effect. It acts mainly on hepatocytes and adipocytes (fat cells), enhancing cellular **glucose uptake and use**, so glucose moves from blood into cells — **hypoglycemia** (lowering). Insulin also stimulates conversion of glucose to glycogen (**glycogenesis**) in target cells. The balance of insulin and glucagon maintains glucose homeostasis.

Prolonged hyperglycemia leads to **diabetes mellitus**, which is associated with loss of glucose through urine and formation of harmful compounds called **ketone bodies**. Diabetic patients are successfully treated with insulin therapy. India has one of the largest numbers of people with diabetes in the world, which is why regular check-ups, exercise and a balanced diet are widely encouraged. (Treatment decisions are always for a doctor.)

> Did you know? Human insulin for patients is now made by genetically engineered bacteria — you will meet this in Class 12 Biotechnology.

check.q: After a large meal, which change is expected?
options: β-cells release more insulin and liver stores glycogen
check.why: Rising blood glucose stimulates β-cells to secrete insulin, which drives glucose into cells and promotes glycogenesis.

sections.md:
The **testes**, a pair in the scrotal sac, are primary sex organs and also endocrine glands. Each is made of **seminiferous tubules** with stromal (interstitial) tissue between them. The **Leydig cells (interstitial cells)** in the intertubular spaces produce a group of hormones called **androgens**, mainly **testosterone**.

Androgens regulate the development, maturation and functions of male accessory sex organs (epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, prostate gland, urethra). They stimulate muscular growth, growth of facial and axillary hair, aggressiveness and a low pitch of voice. They play a major stimulatory role in spermatogenesis, act on the central nervous system to influence male sexual behaviour (libido), and have anabolic effects on protein and carbohydrate metabolism.

Females have a pair of **ovaries** in the abdomen. The ovary is the primary female sex organ, producing one ovum during each menstrual cycle, and two groups of steroid hormones: **estrogen** and **progesterone**. The ovary contains ovarian follicles and stromal tissue. Estrogen is synthesised and secreted mainly by the **growing ovarian follicles**. After ovulation, the ruptured follicle becomes the **corpus luteum**, which secretes mainly **progesterone**.

Estrogen stimulates growth and activity of female secondary sex organs, development of growing ovarian follicles, the appearance of female secondary sex characters (for example, high pitch of voice), mammary gland development, and regulates female sexual behaviour. Progesterone supports **pregnancy**; it also acts on mammary glands, stimulating the formation of alveoli (sac-like structures that store milk) and milk secretion.

You will study reproduction in full in Class 12 — here the key idea is that the gonads are endocrine glands under control of pituitary LH and FSH, which are themselves under control of hypothalamic GnRH.

check.q: Which structure is the main source of progesterone after ovulation?
check.why: After ovulation the ruptured follicle turns into the corpus luteum, whose main secretion is progesterone that supports pregnancy.

sections.h: Hormones of heart, kidney and gut
sections.md:
Some tissues that are not endocrine glands still secrete hormones.

- **Heart**: the atrial wall secretes **atrial natriuretic factor (ANF)**, a peptide. When blood pressure rises, ANF causes blood vessels to dilate, which **lowers blood pressure**. It is a neat counterweight to the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system you studied in the excretion chapter.
- **Kidney**: the juxtaglomerular cells produce **erythropoietin**, a peptide hormone that stimulates **erythropoiesis** — formation of red blood cells. This is why people with chronic kidney disease often become anaemic.
- **Gastrointestinal tract**: endocrine cells in different parts secrete four major peptide hormones:
  - **Gastrin** — acts on gastric glands, stimulating secretion of HCl and pepsinogen.
  - **Secretin** — acts on the exocrine pancreas, stimulating secretion of water and bicarbonate ions.
  - **Cholecystokinin (CCK)** — acts on both pancreas and gall bladder, stimulating pancreatic enzymes and bile juice.
  - **Gastric inhibitory peptide (GIP)** — inhibits gastric secretion and motility.

Several other non-endocrine tissues secrete **growth factors**, essential for normal growth of tissues and their repair or regeneration.

A handy memory hook: 'Gastrin Gets acid, Secretin Sends soda (bicarbonate), CCK Calls the gall bladder, GIP Grinds things to a pause.'

check.q: Which hormone directly stimulates release of bile from the gall bladder?
check.why: Cholecystokinin acts on the gall bladder to release bile and on the pancreas to release digestive enzymes.

sections.h: How hormones act on target cells
sections.md:
A hormone only works on a cell that has a matching **hormone receptor** — a specific protein. Receptors in the **cell membrane** are **membrane-bound receptors**; receptors inside the cell are **intracellular receptors**, mostly **nuclear receptors** in the nucleus. Binding forms a **hormone–receptor complex**, which triggers biochemical changes in the target tissue. Each receptor is specific to one hormone — like a lock that accepts one key. This is why adrenaline flowing past a bone cell does nothing much, while the same molecule makes the heart race.

Based on chemical nature, hormones are grouped as:
1. **Peptide, polypeptide and protein hormones** — insulin, glucagon, pituitary hormones, hypothalamic hormones.
2. **Steroids** — cortisol, testosterone, estradiol, progesterone.
3. **Iodothyronines** — thyroid hormones.
4. **Amino-acid derivatives** — adrenaline (epinephrine).

**Two mechanisms:**
- **Membrane receptors (for water-soluble hormones like proteins and adrenaline)**: these hormones cannot cross the lipid membrane. They bind receptors on the surface, which generate **second messengers** inside the cell — for example **cyclic AMP**, IP₃ or Ca²⁺. The second messenger then regulates cellular metabolism, often by activating enzymes. The hormone itself is the 'first messenger'.
- **Intracellular receptors (for lipid-soluble hormones like steroids and iodothyronines)**: these hormones pass through the membrane, bind receptors inside, and the complex interacts with the **genome**. They mostly regulate **gene expression** or chromosome function, leading to new proteins and physiological effects.

The second-messenger route also explains **amplification**: one hormone molecule activates one receptor, which can produce many cAMP molecules, each activating many enzymes — so a tiny signal yields a large response.

**Feedback control**: most hormone levels are regulated by **negative feedback**. When thyroxine rises, it inhibits release of TRH from the hypothalamus and TSH from the pituitary, so the thyroid slows down. When thyroxine falls, the brake is released. This is exactly how a water-tank float valve or a refrigerator's thermostat works.

check.q: Why do steroid hormones generally act through intracellular receptors?
options: They are too large to bind the membrane
They are lipid-soluble and can cross the plasma membrane
They are made in the nucleus
check.why: Being lipid-soluble, steroids diffuse through the lipid bilayer and bind receptors inside the cell, where the complex regulates genes.

parts.md: Meera's alarm rang at 6 a.m. in Pune. Light poured through the curtains, and her pineal gland — which had kept melatonin high through the night — quietly dialled it down. Her cortisol was already rising, as it does every morning, nudging the liver to release glucose so her brain had fuel before she had even brushed her teeth.

Breakfast was poha and a glass of milk. As glucose entered her blood, the β-cells of her islets released insulin; muscle and fat cells opened their doors to sugar, and the liver tucked the extra away as glycogen. In her duodenum, secretin and CCK told the pancreas and gall bladder to send bicarbonate, enzymes and bile.

At the exam hall, the invigilator announced: 'Phones in your bags.' Meera's heart jumped. Her adrenal medulla sent a burst of adrenaline: pupils widened, heart sped up, glycogen broke down for quick energy. She took three slow breaths, and as the threat passed, the surge faded. Hormones had prepared her body — her calm mind then took charge.

That night, after a long drink of water following cricket in the colony, she noticed she passed less urine than usual after sweating — vasopressin at work. As darkness fell, melatonin rose again. Every hour of her day had been shaped by molecules she never saw.

summary: Hormones are non-nutrient chemicals made in trace amounts that act as intercellular messengers.
Endocrine glands are ductless; the main ones are pituitary, pineal, thyroid, parathyroid, adrenal, pancreas, thymus and gonads.
The hypothalamus links nervous and endocrine systems via releasing and inhibiting hormones (portal system) and via axons to the posterior pituitary.
Anterior pituitary: GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH; pars intermedia: MSH; posterior pituitary releases oxytocin and vasopressin.
GH excess → gigantism (child) or acromegaly (adult); deficiency → dwarfism. ADH deficiency → diabetes insipidus.
Pineal melatonin regulates diurnal rhythm.
Thyroid makes T₃, T₄ (need iodine) and thyrocalcitonin; disorders include goitre, cretinism and Graves' disease.
PTH raises blood Ca²⁺; TCT lowers it.
Thymosins help T-lymphocyte differentiation; the thymus shrinks with age.
Adrenal medulla: adrenaline/noradrenaline (fight or flight); cortex: cortisol, aldosterone, androgens; deficiency → Addison's disease.
Insulin (β-cells) lowers blood glucose; glucagon (α-cells) raises it; prolonged hyperglycemia → diabetes mellitus.
Testes (Leydig cells) make androgens; ovaries make estrogen (follicles) and progesterone (corpus luteum).
Heart (ANF), kidney (erythropoietin) and GI tract (gastrin, secretin, CCK, GIP) also secrete hormones.
Protein hormones use membrane receptors and second messengers like cAMP; steroids and iodothyronines use intracellular receptors and regulate genes.

sections.h: How to use this revision read
sections.md:
Picture the night before your annual exam. Nineteen chapters, five units, hundreds of names — *Funaria, Pheretima, zona fasciculata, Calvin cycle*. Where do you even start?

Start with the **storyline**. Class 11 Biology is really one long story told in five acts:

| Unit | Big question | Chapters |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Diversity in the Living World | What lives on Earth and how do we name and group it? | The Living World; Biological Classification; Plant Kingdom; Animal Kingdom |
| 2. Structural Organisation | How are plants and animals built? | Morphology of Flowering Plants; Anatomy of Flowering Plants; Structural Organisation in Animals |
| 3. Cell: Structure and Function | What is the unit of life and how does it work and divide? | Cell: The Unit of Life; Biomolecules; Cell Cycle and Cell Division |
| 4. Plant Physiology | How do plants make food, release energy and grow? | Photosynthesis in Higher Plants; Respiration in Plants; Plant Growth and Development |
| 5. Human Physiology | How does the human body run? | Breathing; Body Fluids and Circulation; Excretory Products; Locomotion and Movement; Neural Control; Chemical Coordination |

For each unit below you get: the core ideas, the facts examiners love, a figure, and a check. Then a story recap, worked numericals and a practice set at the end. Read actively: cover the tables, recall, then peek.

> Revision rule of three: understand it, draw it, explain it aloud to someone. If you can do all three, you own it.

sections.h: Unit 1 — Diversity in the living world
sections.md:
**The Living World.** Living things grow, reproduce, metabolise, respond to stimuli and show cellular organisation. **Metabolism**, **cellular organisation** and **consciousness/response to stimuli** are defining features, while growth and reproduction alone are not (crystals grow, mules don't reproduce). Naming uses **binomial nomenclature** from Carolus Linnaeus: genus with capital letter, species epithet in small letters, both italicised or underlined — *Mangifera indica*; the author's name is abbreviated after it (*Mangifera indica* Linn.). Rules are set by ICBN (plants) and ICZN (animals). The **taxonomic hierarchy** runs Kingdom → Phylum/Division → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species; going up, members share fewer characters. Example: mango — Plantae, Angiospermae (division), Dicotyledonae, Sapindales, Anacardiaceae, *Mangifera*, *indica*. Housefly — Animalia, Arthropoda, Insecta, Diptera, Muscidae, *Musca*, *domestica*. Taxonomic aids include herbaria, botanical gardens (e.g. the Indian Botanic Garden at Howrah), museums, zoological parks and keys (paired contrasting statements called couplets).

**Biological Classification.** Aristotle used simple plant and animal traits; Linnaeus had two kingdoms. R.H. Whittaker's (1969) **five-kingdom** system: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia — based on cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction and phylogeny.
- *Monera*: bacteria (prokaryotes) — spherical cocci, rod bacilli, comma vibrios, spiral spirilla. Archaebacteria live in extreme habitats (halophiles, thermoacidophiles, methanogens — the last in cattle guts, producing biogas). Cyanobacteria (*Nostoc*, *Anabaena*) fix nitrogen in heterocysts. Mycoplasma lack a cell wall and are the smallest living cells.
- *Protista*: unicellular eukaryotes — chrysophytes (diatoms, whose walls form diatomaceous earth), dinoflagellates (red tides), euglenoids (pellicle; mixotrophic), slime moulds (saprophytic, form plasmodium), protozoans — amoeboid, flagellated (*Trypanosoma*, sleeping sickness), ciliated (*Paramoecium*) and sporozoans (*Plasmodium*, malaria).
- *Fungi*: chitin walls, heterotrophic; Phycomycetes (*Rhizopus*, *Albugo*), Ascomycetes (sac fungi — yeast, *Penicillium*, morels), Basidiomycetes (mushrooms, rusts, smuts), Deuteromycetes (imperfect fungi, *Alternaria*).
- Viruses (D.J. Ivanowsky, 1892; W.M. Stanley crystallised TMV), viroids (T.O. Diener, 1971 — free RNA without a protein coat), prions and lichens (alga + fungus, pollution indicators) are kept outside the five kingdoms.

**Plant Kingdom.** Algae (Chlorophyceae — green, starch; Phaeophyceae — brown, laminarin, mannitol; Rhodophyceae — red, floridean starch, r-phycoerythrin) → Bryophytes (liverworts and mosses; amphibians of the plant kingdom; dominant gametophyte; *Sphagnum* gives peat) → Pteridophytes (first vascular plants; dominant sporophyte; ferns, horsetails, *Selaginella* is heterosporous) → Gymnosperms (naked seeds; *Cycas*, *Pinus*) → Angiosperms (seeds in fruits; double fertilisation; triploid endosperm). Life cycles: haplontic (*Volvox*, *Spirogyra*), diplontic (seed plants, *Fucus*), haplo-diplontic (bryophytes, pteridophytes, *Ectocarpus*).

**Animal Kingdom.** Basis of classification: levels of organisation (cellular, tissue, organ, organ system), symmetry (asymmetrical, radial, bilateral), germ layers (diploblastic/triploblastic), coelom (acoelomate, pseudocoelomate, coelomate), segmentation (metamerism), notochord. Phyla from Porifera through Chordata; the vertebrates include Cyclostomata, Chondrichthyes, Osteichthyes, Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves and Mammalia.

check.q: Which group is called the 'amphibians of the plant kingdom'?
check.why: Bryophytes live on land but need water for fertilisation, so they are called the amphibians of the plant kingdom.

sections.h: Unit 1 quick table — animal phyla at a glance
sections.md:
Examiners love 'give two distinguishing features and one example'. This table covers the non-chordate phyla and chordates in order. Read it across, then try to fill it from memory.

Chordates have three fundamental features — a **notochord**, a **dorsal hollow nerve cord** and **paired pharyngeal gill slits** — plus a post-anal tail at some stage. Subphyla: Urochordata (notochord only in larval tail, *Ascidia*), Cephalochordata (notochord head to tail throughout life, *Branchiostoma*), Vertebrata (notochord replaced by vertebral column). All vertebrates are chordates, but not all chordates are vertebrates.

Vertebrate classes in one line each: **Cyclostomata** — jawless, sucking circular mouth, ectoparasites (*Petromyzon*); **Chondrichthyes** — cartilaginous, placoid scales, no air bladder (*Scoliodon*, *Pristis*); **Osteichthyes** — bony, operculum, air bladder (*Labeo*, rohu); **Amphibia** — moist skin, three-chambered heart, external fertilisation (*Rana*); **Reptilia** — dry scaly skin, mostly three-chambered heart (crocodiles four) (*Naja*); **Aves** — feathers, beak, pneumatic bones, four-chambered heart, homeothermic (*Corvus*, *Pavo*); **Mammalia** — mammary glands, hair, external ears (pinnae), four-chambered heart, mostly viviparous (*Macropus*, *Panthera*).

sections.h: Unit 2 — Structural organisation in plants and animals
sections.md:
**Morphology of Flowering Plants.** Roots: tap root (dicots), fibrous (monocots), adventitious; modifications for storage (carrot, turnip, sweet potato), support (prop roots of banyan, stilt roots of maize and sugarcane) and respiration (pneumatophores of *Rhizophora*). Stems: underground modifications (potato tuber, ginger rhizome, onion bulb, *Colocasia* corm), tendrils (cucumber, grape), thorns (*Citrus*, *Bougainvillea*), phylloclades (*Opuntia*), runners and offsets for propagation. Leaves: simple/compound (pinnate in neem, palmate in silk cotton), venation (reticulate in dicots, parallel in monocots), phyllotaxy (alternate in China rose, opposite in guava, whorled in *Alstonia*); modifications into tendrils (pea), spines (cactus), and insect-trapping pitchers. Inflorescence: racemose (main axis keeps growing) vs cymose (main axis ends in a flower). Flower: calyx, corolla, androecium, gynoecium; symmetry actinomorphic or zygomorphic; ovary position — hypogynous, perigynous, epigynous; aestivation — valvate (*Calotropis*), twisted (China rose), imbricate (*Cassia*), vexillary (pea); placentation — marginal (pea), axile (tomato), parietal (mustard), basal (sunflower), free central (*Dianthus*). Fruits develop from the ovary (parthenocarpic fruits without fertilisation); seeds have seed coat, embryo and, in many, endosperm. Families to know: **Fabaceae** (pea; vexillary, diadelphous stamens), **Solanaceae** (potato, brinjal; axile placentation, swollen placenta), **Liliaceae** (onion, tulip; perianth of six tepals, trilocular ovary) with floral formulae.

**Anatomy of Flowering Plants.** Tissues: meristematic (apical, intercalary, lateral) and permanent — simple (parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma) and complex (xylem: tracheids, vessels, fibres, parenchyma; phloem: sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and fibres). Tissue systems: epidermal (cuticle, stomata with guard cells — bean-shaped in dicots, dumb-bell-shaped in grasses — and trichomes), ground, vascular (radial, conjoint, open/closed). Dicot vs monocot root and stem are classic comparison questions: dicot stem has vascular bundles in a ring, open with cambium; monocot stem has scattered, closed bundles. Dicot leaf is dorsiventral with palisade and spongy mesophyll; monocot leaf is isobilateral, with bulliform cells. **Secondary growth**: vascular cambium (intrafascicular + interfascicular) and cork cambium (phellogen) producing periderm; annual rings (spring/early wood and autumn/late wood); heartwood (dark, non-conducting) vs sapwood; lenticels for gas exchange.

**Structural Organisation in Animals.** Four tissue types: epithelial (simple squamous, cuboidal, columnar, ciliated; compound; glandular; junctions — tight, adhering, gap), connective (loose, dense, specialised — cartilage, bone, blood), muscular (skeletal, smooth, cardiac), neural. Then the frog (*Rana tigrina* in the revised book) — morphology and organ systems: digestive, respiratory (skin, buccal cavity, lungs), circulatory (three-chambered heart, hepatic and renal portal systems), excretory (ureotelic), nervous and reproductive systems. The frog is cold-blooded, shows camouflage, and undergoes hibernation and aestivation.

right.title: Monocot stem
points: Water-containing cavities in bundles; no secondary growth usually

check.q: In which placentation are ovules attached to a central axis in a multilocular ovary?
check.why: In axile placentation the placenta is axial and ovules attach to it in a multilocular ovary, as in China rose, tomato and lemon.

sections.h: Unit 3 — The cell, its molecules and its division
sections.md:
**Cell: The Unit of Life.** Cell theory (Schleiden, Schwann, then Virchow's *omnis cellula e cellula*). Prokaryotes lack a membrane-bound nucleus; they have a nucleoid, plasmids, 70S ribosomes, mesosomes; Gram-positive and Gram-negative cell envelopes. Eukaryotic organelles: plasma membrane (fluid mosaic model — Singer and Nicolson, 1972; transport passive, active via the Na⁺/K⁺ pump), cell wall (cellulose, middle lamella of calcium pectate), endomembrane system (ER — rough makes proteins, smooth makes lipids; Golgi packages and makes glycoproteins; lysosomes with hydrolases; vacuoles with tonoplast), mitochondria (powerhouse; own DNA, 70S ribosomes, cristae), plastids (chloroplasts, chromoplasts, leucoplasts), 80S ribosomes, cytoskeleton, cilia and flagella (9+2 axoneme), centrosome (centrioles with 9 triplet fibrils, cartwheel), nucleus with nucleolus and pores, chromosomes classified by centromere position (metacentric, sub-metacentric, acrocentric, telocentric). Microbodies include peroxisomes and glyoxysomes.

**Biomolecules.** Chemical analysis reveals small biomolecules (acid-soluble) and macromolecules (acid-insoluble): proteins, polysaccharides, nucleic acids, lipids (lipids are not strictly polymers but appear in the insoluble fraction because they form membrane vesicles). Proteins are polymers of 20 amino acids (heteropolymers); collagen is the most abundant protein in animals and RuBisCO in the biosphere. Polysaccharides: cellulose (homopolymer of glucose), starch (forms helices that hold iodine — blue colour), glycogen, inulin, chitin. Nucleic acids are polynucleotides of nucleotides (sugar + phosphate + base). Protein structure levels: primary to quaternary (haemoglobin has 4 subunits). **Enzymes**: lower activation energy; affected by temperature, pH and substrate concentration (Vmax and Km); inhibition (competitive — e.g. malonate inhibits succinic dehydrogenase); classes — oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, ligases; cofactors — prosthetic groups (haem in peroxidase), coenzymes (NAD, NADP from niacin), metal ions (Zn²⁺ in carboxypeptidase).

**Cell Cycle and Cell Division.** Interphase (G₁, S, G₂) takes over 95% of the cycle; G₀ is quiescent. A human cell in culture divides about once in 24 h; yeast in about 90 min. **Mitosis**: prophase, metaphase (chromosomes on the metaphase plate — best stage to study morphology), anaphase, telophase, then cytokinesis (cell plate in plants, furrow in animals) — equational division keeping chromosome number; significance: growth, repair, cell replacement. **Meiosis**: two divisions; prophase I has leptotene, zygotene (synapsis, synaptonemal complex), pachytene (crossing over by recombinase), diplotene (chiasmata), diakinesis (terminalisation). Meiosis halves the chromosome number at meiosis I and creates variation.

sections.md:
**Photosynthesis in Higher Plants.** Early experiments: Priestley (candle, mouse and mint — plants restore air), Ingenhousz (sunlight needed; only green parts), Sachs (glucose and starch made in chloroplasts), Engelmann (action spectrum with *Cladophora* and aerobic bacteria — blue and red light), Cornelius van Niel (O₂ comes from water). Pigments: chlorophyll a (main), chlorophyll b, xanthophylls, carotenoids. Light reactions in the **grana** (thylakoids): PS II (P680) and PS I (P700), photolysis of water releasing O₂, electron transport (Z-scheme), and **chemiosmotic** ATP synthesis as protons move through ATP synthase (CF₀–CF₁). Cyclic photophosphorylation (PS I only) makes ATP but no NADPH. Products: ATP and NADPH. Dark (biosynthetic) reactions in the **stroma**: the **Calvin cycle** (Melvin Calvin, using ¹⁴C) — carboxylation of RuBP by RuBisCO, reduction, regeneration; first stable product a 3-carbon PGA; making one glucose needs 18 ATP and 12 NADPH. **C₄ plants** (maize, sugarcane, sorghum) show Kranz anatomy and fix CO₂ first into a 4-carbon acid (OAA) via PEP case in mesophyll, then release it in bundle-sheath cells; they avoid **photorespiration**, the wasteful oxygenation of RuBP in C₃ plants. Factors: light, CO₂, temperature, water — Blackman's law of limiting factors (1905).

**Respiration in Plants.** Glycolysis (EMP pathway) in the cytoplasm: glucose → 2 pyruvate, net 2 ATP + 2 NADH. Anaerobic: fermentation to ethanol (yeast) or lactic acid (muscles). Aerobic: link reaction to acetyl CoA, **Krebs cycle** (citric acid cycle; Hans Krebs) in mitochondrial matrix, then the **electron transport system** and oxidative phosphorylation on the inner membrane (Complexes I–IV, cytochrome c, ubiquinone), O₂ being the final acceptor. Theoretical yield ~38 ATP per glucose (textbook assumption). Respiration is an **amphibolic pathway** — it both breaks down and supplies building blocks. **Respiratory quotient** RQ = CO₂ evolved/O₂ consumed: 1 for carbohydrates, about 0.7 for fats, about 0.9 for proteins.

**Plant Growth and Development.** Growth is indeterminate (open), measured as arithmetic (Lt = L₀ + rt) or geometric (W₁ = W₀eʳᵗ); sigmoid growth curve. Conditions: water, oxygen, nutrients, temperature. Differentiation, dedifferentiation, redifferentiation; plasticity (heterophylly in cotton, coriander, larkspur, buttercup). **Plant growth regulators**: auxins (IAA, IBA, 2,4-D; apical dominance, rooting, parthenocarpy, weedicide), gibberellins (bolting, stem elongation, malting, sugarcane yield), cytokinins (kinetin, zeatin; cell division, delay senescence), ethylene (fruit ripening, a gas; ethephon), abscisic acid (stress hormone; stomatal closure, dormancy).

check.why: Ethylene is a simple gaseous regulator that hastens fruit ripening and is used commercially to ripen bananas and mangoes.

sections.md:
**Breathing and Exchange of Gases.** Human respiratory pathway: nostrils → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli. Breathing: inspiration (diaphragm and external intercostals contract, volume up, pressure down) and expiration. Volumes: tidal volume about 500 mL; IRV 2500–3000 mL; ERV 1000–1100 mL; RV 1100–1200 mL; vital capacity = ERV + TV + IRV; total lung capacity = VC + RV. A healthy adult breathes 12–16 times a minute, so 6000–8000 mL per minute. Gas exchange by diffusion across a thin membrane; pO₂ in alveoli about 104 mm Hg, in deoxygenated blood 40. About 97% of O₂ is carried by haemoglobin; the **oxygen dissociation curve** is sigmoid. CO₂ travels mostly as bicarbonate (about 70%, helped by carbonic anhydrase), 20–25% as carbamino-haemoglobin, about 7% dissolved. Regulation by the respiratory rhythm centre in the medulla and pneumotaxic centre in the pons. Disorders: asthma, emphysema, occupational lung diseases (in stone-crushing and grinding industries).

**Body Fluids and Circulation.** Blood: plasma (55%) and formed elements; RBCs (5–5.5 million per mm³; life about 120 days), WBCs (6000–8000 per mm³; neutrophils most, basophils least), platelets (1.5–3.5 lakh per mm³). ABO and Rh grouping; O is universal donor, AB universal recipient; erythroblastosis foetalis in Rh-negative mothers. Lymph carries fats from lacteals. Clotting cascade: thrombokinase → prothrombin → thrombin → fibrinogen → fibrin, needing Ca²⁺. Heart: four chambers; SA node is the pacemaker; AV node, bundle of His, Purkinje fibres; cardiac cycle about 0.8 s at 72 beats/min; stroke volume about 70 mL; cardiac output about 5 L/min; heart sounds lub (AV valves close) and dub (semilunar valves close); ECG waves P (atrial depolarisation), QRS (ventricular depolarisation), T (ventricular repolarisation). Double circulation. Disorders: hypertension (above 140/90), coronary artery disease, angina, heart failure.

**Excretory Products and their Elimination.** Ammonotelic (bony fish), ureotelic (mammals), uricotelic (birds, reptiles) animals. Excretory structures: protonephridia (flatworms), nephridia (earthworm), Malpighian tubules (insects), green glands (prawn). Nephron: glomerulus, Bowman's capsule, PCT, loop of Henle, DCT, collecting duct; cortical and juxtamedullary nephrons. Urine formation: filtration (GFR about 125 mL/min, about 180 L/day), reabsorption (about 99% of filtrate), secretion (H⁺, K⁺, NH₃). Counter-current mechanism (loop of Henle and vasa recta) concentrates urine, with NaCl and urea building a gradient. Regulation by ADH, the renin–angiotensin system (JGA) and ANF. Micturition is a reflex. Disorders: uremia, renal calculi, glomerulonephritis; haemodialysis and transplantation.

sections.md:
**Locomotion and Movement.** Types of movement: amoeboid (macrophages), ciliary (trachea, oviduct), muscular. Skeletal muscle structure: fascicles → muscle fibres (syncytial, with sarcoplasmic reticulum storing Ca²⁺) → myofibrils with **sarcomeres** (between Z lines); A band (myosin, dark, anisotropic), I band (actin, light, isotropic). Actin filaments carry tropomyosin and troponin; each myosin monomer (meromyosin) has a head with ATPase activity. **Sliding filament theory**: a nerve impulse releases acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, an action potential spreads, Ca²⁺ is released from sarcoplasmic reticulum, binds troponin, exposing actin sites; myosin heads (using ATP) form cross-bridges and pull actin toward the centre, shortening the sarcomere while A band length stays the same. Red fibres (myoglobin, many mitochondria) vs white fibres. Skeleton: 206 bones — axial (80: skull 22, hyoid, ear ossicles, vertebral column 26, sternum, 12 pairs of ribs) and appendicular (126). Joints: fibrous (skull sutures), cartilaginous (between vertebrae), synovial (ball and socket, hinge, pivot, gliding, saddle). Disorders: myasthenia gravis, muscular dystrophy, tetany, arthritis, osteoporosis, gout.

**Neural Control and Coordination.** Neurons: dendrites, cell body with Nissl's granules, axon; multipolar, bipolar, unipolar; myelinated (nodes of Ranvier, saltatory conduction) vs non-myelinated. Resting potential maintained by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in); a stimulus opens Na⁺ channels → depolarisation → action potential propagates. Synapses: electrical and chemical (neurotransmitters such as acetylcholine released from vesicles, binding receptors across the cleft). CNS: forebrain (cerebrum with corpus callosum, thalamus, hypothalamus, limbic system), midbrain, hindbrain (pons, cerebellum, medulla); brain stem = midbrain + pons + medulla. The revised book has removed reflex action and sensory organs from this chapter, so check your syllabus.

**Chemical Coordination and Integration.** Hypothalamus (releasing and inhibiting hormones) → pituitary (adenohypophysis: GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH; neurohypophysis stores oxytocin and vasopressin) → target glands; pineal melatonin (day–night rhythm); thyroid T₃/T₄ and TCT (iodine deficiency → goitre; hypothyroidism in pregnancy → cretinism); parathyroid PTH (raises blood Ca²⁺); thymus thymosins (immunity); adrenal cortex (glucocorticoids like cortisol, mineralocorticoids like aldosterone) and medulla (adrenaline, noradrenaline — 'fight or flight'); pancreas insulin (lowers blood glucose) and glucagon (raises it); gonads; hormones of heart (ANF), kidney (erythropoietin) and gut (gastrin, secretin, CCK, GIP). Mechanisms: membrane receptors and second messengers (cAMP, Ca²⁺) for protein hormones; intracellular receptors and gene expression for steroid hormones and iodothyronines.

sections.md:
**Diagrams win marks.** Practise these until you can draw them in under three minutes: prokaryotic cell, plant and animal cell, mitochondrion and chloroplast, stages of mitosis, T.S. of dicot and monocot root and stem, the Z-scheme, Krebs cycle outline, nephron, human heart sectional view, sarcomere, neuron, structure of a synapse and the location of endocrine glands.

**Comparison tables** are very common questions. Keep a list: prokaryote vs eukaryote; mitosis vs meiosis; C₃ vs C₄; aerobic vs anaerobic respiration; dicot vs monocot anatomy; open vs closed circulation; ammonotelism vs ureotelism; red vs white muscle fibres; peptide vs steroid hormone action.

**Number facts** to memorise (rounded textbook values): tidal volume 500 mL; GFR 125 mL/min; cardiac cycle 0.8 s; RBCs 5–5.5 million/mm³; 206 bones; RuBisCO is the most abundant enzyme on Earth; 18 ATP + 12 NADPH per glucose in Calvin cycle; RQ of fats about 0.7.

**Traps:**
- *Viruses* are not placed in any of the five kingdoms.
- *Fats* are not polymers, yet appear in the acid-insoluble fraction.
- *Oxytocin and vasopressin* are made in the hypothalamus, stored and released by the posterior pituitary.
- *Photorespiration* happens in C₃ plants, not C₄.
- *Cardiac output* = stroke volume × heart rate: 70 mL × 72 = 5040 mL ≈ 5 L per minute.
- In meiosis, chromosome number halves at **meiosis I**, not meiosis II.

> Did you know? The revised (rationalised) NCERT books removed several chapters such as Transport in Plants and Mineral Nutrition. Always check the current syllabus your board lists before revising old guidebooks.

check.q: Stroke volume 70 mL and heart rate 72 per minute give cardiac output of about:
check.why: 70 mL × 72 = 5040 mL per minute, which is about 5 litres per minute.

parts.md: At 6 a.m. Riya jogs along the Marine Drive promenade. Her diaphragm flattens with each breath, about 500 mL of tidal air rushes in, and oxygen diffuses from alveoli (pO₂ about 104 mm Hg) into blood. Haemoglobin picks it up along its S-shaped dissociation curve. Her SA node quickens the beat; stroke volume and heart rate rise, so cardiac output climbs far above the resting 5 L per minute.

In her calf muscles, acetylcholine crosses the neuromuscular junction, Ca²⁺ floods out of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, troponin shifts, and myosin heads pull on actin — the sliding filament story. When oxygen runs short in a sprint, her muscle cells switch to lactic acid fermentation, giving that familiar burning feeling. Glucose is broken down by glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and the electron transport system to refill her ATP.

At school, the neem tree outside the lab is doing the opposite trade. In its chloroplasts, PS II splits water and releases the O₂ Riya breathed; the Calvin cycle uses 18 ATP and 12 NADPH to build each glucose. The tree's cambium adds a thin ring of wood each year, and auxin from its shoot tip keeps side buds in check. Plant and person are linked through gases, sugar and energy.

At night, Riya's kidneys keep filtering about 125 mL of plasma a minute, reabsorbing nearly all of it, while ADH from the posterior pituitary saves water. Her pineal gland releases melatonin as the room darkens. Inside her skin cells, a few divide by mitosis to repair a scraped knee. Breathing, circulation, excretion, movement, nerves, hormones, photosynthesis and the cell cycle all happen in one ordinary day, and that is the whole book.

workedExamples.q: Vital capacity of a student is 4600 mL, tidal volume 500 mL and ERV 1100 mL. Find IRV.
A cell has 2n = 24 chromosomes. How many chromosomes and chromatids are present at metaphase of mitosis and in each cell after meiosis II?
steps: After S phase each chromosome has 2 chromatids; number of chromosomes stays 24
Meiosis halves the number: each final cell has n = 12 chromosomes, each with one chromatid
workedExamples.answer: Mitotic metaphase: 24 chromosomes, 48 chromatids; after meiosis II: 12 chromosomes

workedExamples.q: How many turns of the Calvin cycle make one glucose, and how many ATP are used?
steps: Each turn fixes one CO₂; glucose has 6 carbons, so 6 turns
Each turn uses 3 ATP and 2 NADPH

workedExamples.q: Tripalmitin is oxidised using 145 O₂ and releasing 102 CO₂. Find its RQ.
A person's heart rate is 75 per minute and stroke volume 70 mL. Find cardiac output and the duration of one cardiac cycle.
If GFR is 125 mL/min, how much filtrate forms per day, and roughly how much urine if 99% is reabsorbed?
workedExamples.answer: About 180 L of filtrate and about 1.5–1.8 L of urine per day

summary: Class 11 Biology has five units: diversity, structural organisation, cell, plant physiology and human physiology.
Binomial nomenclature and the taxonomic hierarchy organise life; Whittaker proposed five kingdoms in 1969.
Viruses, viroids, prions and lichens lie outside the five kingdoms.
Plant kingdom moves from algae to bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms.
Animals are classified by organisation, symmetry, germ layers, coelom, segmentation and notochord.
Know root, stem and leaf modifications, floral features and the families Fabaceae, Solanaceae and Liliaceae.
Dicot and monocot anatomy differ in vascular bundle arrangement and secondary growth.
Cells: prokaryotic vs eukaryotic, organelles and the fluid mosaic membrane.
Enzymes lower activation energy; competitive inhibitors resemble the substrate.
Mitosis keeps chromosome number; meiosis halves it and creates variation through crossing over.
Photosynthesis: light reactions make ATP and NADPH; the Calvin cycle fixes CO₂; C₄ plants avoid photorespiration.
Respiration: glycolysis, Krebs cycle, ETS; RQ depends on substrate.
Plant growth regulators: auxin, gibberellin, cytokinin, ethylene and ABA.
Human physiology covers breathing, circulation, excretion, movement, nerves and hormones.
Draw, compare and memorise key numbers to score.

rd-school-c11-business-b.revision-practi.title: Class 11 Business Studies: The Whole Book in One Sitting
rd-school-c11-business-b.revision-practi.subtitle: From a chaiwala's stall to a multinational: every chapter, revised as one connected story

sections.h: How to use this revision read
sections.md:
Picture Meera, who runs a small tea stall outside Pune railway station. Over ten years her stall becomes a partnership, then a company, borrows from a bank, insures its warehouse, sells on an app, exports masala chai to Dubai and runs a scholarship for local girls. **Every chapter of Class 11 Business Studies is a stop on Meera's journey.** That is the trick of revising this book: do not memorise ten separate lists — remember one growing business.

The book has two halves:

1. **Foundations of Business** — what business is, its forms, public and private enterprises, business services, emerging modes (e-business, outsourcing) and social responsibility and ethics.
2. **Finance and Trade** — sources of finance, small business and entrepreneurship, internal trade and international business.

For each chapter below you get: the core idea, the lists examiners love, the usual traps, and one check. At the end are a story recap, a summary sheet and a practice paper. A smart plan: read one section, close the screen, and write the key list from memory. If you can write it, you know it.

> Exam tip: in Business Studies, the *heading* of each point earns half the mark and a one-line explanation earns the other half. Never write a heading alone.

sections.md:
**Economic activities** are done to earn a living; **non-economic** activities are done out of love, duty or social reasons (a mother cooking for her family). Economic activities are of three kinds: **business**, **profession** (doctor, lawyer, CA — needs specialised training and membership of a professional body) and **employment** (working for someone else for a wage or salary).

**History of trade in India.** Indian merchants traded by land and sea for thousands of years — the Silk Route linked India with China and Central Asia, and ports such as Tamralipti, Bharuch and Muziris connected India with the Roman world and South-East Asia. Instruments like the hundi (an indigenous bill of exchange) and merchant guilds (shreni) supported this trade.

**Characteristics of business:** economic activity; production or procurement of goods and services; sale or exchange; dealing in goods and services on a regular basis; profit earning; uncertainty of return; and element of risk.

**Objectives** are multiple, not just profit: market standing, innovation, productivity, physical and financial resources, earning profits, manager performance, worker performance and attitude, and social responsibility.

**Classification of business activities**

| Industry | Commerce |
|---|---|
| Primary (extractive, genetic) | Trade (internal, external) |
| Secondary (manufacturing, construction) | Auxiliaries to trade |
| Tertiary (service) | |

Manufacturing is analytical (oil refining), synthetical (cement), processing (sugar) or assembling (cars). **Auxiliaries to trade** remove hindrances: transport (place), banking (finance), insurance (risk), warehousing (time), advertising (information).

**Business risk** — causes: natural (floods), human (theft, strikes), economic (demand change), and others (political changes). Speculative risks have chance of gain *and* loss; pure risks have only loss.

**Starting a business** — factors: selection of line of business, size, form of ownership, location, financing, physical facilities, plant layout, competent workforce, tax planning, and launching.
keyTerms: Auxiliaries to trade — services that support trade (transport, banking, insurance, warehousing, advertising)
Genetic industry — rearing plants and animals for reproduction, e.g. nurseries, poultry
Speculative risk — may bring profit or loss

check.q: A cement factory combining limestone, clay and gypsum is an example of which manufacturing type?
check.why: Synthetical industries combine several raw materials into one new product, which is exactly what cement making does.

sections.md:
Meera's choice of form decides who owns, who controls and who bears the loss.

**Sole proprietorship** — one owner. Features: formation and closure easy, unlimited liability, sole risk bearer and profit recipient, control, no separate entity, lack of business continuity. Merits: quick decisions, confidentiality, direct incentive, sense of accomplishment, ease of formation. Limitations: limited resources, limited life, unlimited liability, limited managerial ability.

**Joint Hindu Family (HUF) business** — governed by Hindu Succession Act, 1956; the eldest member, the **karta**, manages; co-parceners have limited liability except the karta, whose liability is unlimited; continuity on death.

**Partnership** — governed by the Indian Partnership Act, 1932. Minimum 2 partners; maximum 50 (Companies Rules, 2014). Unlimited liability, mutual agency, shared risk. Types of partners: active, sleeping, secret, nominal, partner by estoppel. Registration is optional but an unregistered firm cannot sue third parties. A **Limited Liability Partnership (LLP)** (2008 Act) blends partnership flexibility with limited liability.

**Cooperative society** — voluntary membership, legal status after registration, limited liability, democratic control (one member, one vote), service motive. Types: consumer, producer, marketing, farmers', credit, housing — think Amul, a milk cooperative.

**Joint stock company** — an artificial person created by law, separate legal entity, perpetual succession, common seal (now optional), limited liability, transfer of shares, risk bearing spread over shareholders. **Private company**: min 2 members, max 200, restricts transfer of shares, cannot invite public to subscribe. **Public company**: min 7 members, no maximum, freely transferable shares. A **One Person Company** has a single member. Formation stages: promotion, incorporation, and (for public companies raising money) capital subscription.

**Choosing a form** depends on cost and ease of setting up, liability, continuity, management ability, capital needed, degree of control and nature of business.

check.q: Which partner is NOT really a partner but lets his name be used, becoming liable to outsiders?
check.why: A nominal partner lends name and reputation without investing or managing, yet is liable to third parties who trusted that name.

sections.h: Ch 3 · Private, Public and Global Enterprises
sections.md:
**Public sector enterprises** are owned (wholly or mostly) by the government. Three forms:

- **Departmental undertakings** — part of a ministry, financed from the budget, accountable to the ministry, staffed by civil servants (Railways in the classic textbook example, Posts). Good for strategic control; weak in flexibility.
- **Statutory corporations** — created by a special Act of Parliament, separate legal entity, financially independent, own staff (LIC, ONGC in origin). Autonomy but the Act is rigid to change.
- **Government companies** — registered under the Companies Act with at least 51% of paid-up capital held by government (SAIL, BHEL). Easy to form and flexible, but can drift from public purpose.

**Changing role of the public sector since 1991:** development of infrastructure, regional balance, economies of scale, check over concentration of economic power, import substitution. The 1991 policy reduced reserved industries, used disinvestment, made sick PSUs referable to BIFR, and signed **MoUs** for autonomy with accountability.

**Global enterprises (MNCs)** — huge capital resources, foreign collaboration, advanced technology, product innovation through R&D, marketing strategies, expansion of market territory, centralised control from the headquarters.

**Joint ventures** — two or more firms pooling resources for a common purpose. Benefits: increased resources and capacity, access to new markets and distribution networks, access to technology, innovation, low cost of production, established brand name. **Public-Private Partnership (PPP)** — government and private sector share risk and reward, e.g. highways and airports.

check.q: A government company must have at least what share of paid-up capital held by government?
check.why: Under the Companies Act a government company is one in which the government holds not less than 51% of the paid-up share capital.

sections.md:
Services are **intangible, inconsistent, inseparable** (produced and consumed together), **inventory-less** (cannot be stored) and need **involvement** of the customer — the famous five Is.

**Types:** business services (banking, insurance, transport, warehousing, communication), social services (health, education by NGOs) and personal services (tourism, restaurants).

**Banking** — accepts deposits and lends. Types: commercial, cooperative, specialised (EXIM, NABARD), and the central bank (RBI). Functions: accepting deposits, lending (overdraft, cash credit, loans), cheque facility, remittance, allied services. **E-banking**: NEFT, RTGS, IMPS, UPI, debit and credit cards — saving time and cost for both customer and bank.

**Insurance** — a contract where the insurer promises to compensate loss in return for a premium. Principles: **utmost good faith**, **insurable interest**, **indemnity** (not for life insurance), **proximate cause**, **subrogation**, **contribution** and **mitigation of loss**. Types: life (whole life, endowment, joint life, annuity, children's endowment), fire, marine (hull, cargo, freight).

**Communication services** — postal (letters, registered post, parcels, speed post, courier) and telecom (cellular, fixed line, cable, VSAT, DTH).

**Transportation** removes the hindrance of place. **Warehousing** removes the hindrance of time. Types: private, public, bonded (goods kept before customs duty is paid), government, cooperative. Functions: consolidation, break the bulk, stock piling, value-added services, price stabilisation, financing (warehouse receipts).
